## Output Contract Philosophy

The framework should enforce required semantics and stable anchors, but it should not force shallow or overly rigid templates.

Artifacts should be:

- richly detailed when needed
- compact when the work is simple
- easy for other agents to continue
- explicit about uncertainty, dependencies, and handoffs

Every major artifact should have stable anchors such as:

- identity (`Change ID`, `wave-id`, persona name, etc.)
- status
- scope
- dependencies
- evidence refs
- next actions or handoffs

Everything beyond that should be allowed to expand naturally based on the work.
Lists of tasks, guardrails, required semantics, and review checks should be treated as minimum anchors and illustrative categories, not as a ceiling on how much detail or how many items an agent may include when the work warrants more.

Output contracts should also be version-aware enough that later prompts and tooling can detect missing anchors or stale semantics and report clear diagnostics.

## Wave Model

Waves are execution and knowledge-transfer phases, not merely concurrency buckets.

### Canonical Wave Goals

A wave artifact exists to preserve the minimum durable truth needed for multi-agent execution and continuation:

- **Operational truth:** what work is in scope for this wave, what state it is in, and what outputs are expected or already produced.
- **Coordination truth:** who is coordinating, which participants and lanes are active, how work is allocated, and which dependencies or checkpoints gate progress.
- **Assumption truth:** which assumptions and interfaces are frozen, tentative, confirmed, or invalidated, and which changes or tasks they affect.
- **Disposition truth:** which changes or tasks completed, blocked, deferred, moved, retried, or were superseded, and why.
- **C

arry-forward truth:** what remains part of the same `Change ID`, what must move into the next wave, and what conditions make the next wave ready or not ready.
- **Handoff truth:** enough state, rationale, findings, and review status that another agent can continue or challenge the wave without reconstructing missing context from scratch.

These goals define the contract for wave artifacts and reconciliation helpers. Section layouts may vary, but these truths must remain recoverable.

- a wave can contain one small fix or many compatible feature slices
- a wave can contain multiple workstreams when their assumptions are compatible
- only one wave should normally be active per `change-id` at a time
- the wave coordinator owns execution order, agent allocation, review checkpoints, and wave completion
- small waves and large waves should use the same scalable artifact model: the `## Changes` section can stay compact for a one-line fix or the change docs can expand into nested workstreams for a large feature bundle
- waves should make partial failure, retries, deferred changes, and moved changes explicit so downstream agents can tell what actually completed

### Wave Orchestration Contract

Wave collaboration should be explicit enough that multiple agents can run the same wave consistently rather than improvising different coordination models.

Each active wave should make the following orchestration concerns explicit:

- **Coordinator:** the role or owner that admits work into the wave, allocates work, enforces dependencies, and declares the wave complete
- **Roster:** which generic roles and project personas are participating, and whether they are implementing, reviewing, challenging, or approving
- **Allocation:** which changes, tasks, or workstreams belong to which participant and what dependencies must clear before they start
- **Synchronization:** when participants report findings, blockers, invalidated assumptions, and outputs back to the coordinator
- **Escalatio

n:** what conditions force replanning, reassignment, added review, or wave supersession
- **Closure:** what must be true for the wave to close and what happens to incomplete, deferred, moved, or retried work

The intended lifecycle for an active wave is:

- **Admission** — choose the work that belongs in the wave and verify assumptions, dependencies, and entry criteria
- **Allocation** — assign changes, tasks, and review lanes to agents and personas
- **Execution** — run the admitted work while preserving explicit status, blockers, and assumptions
- **Reconciliation** — consolidate outputs, record invalidated assumptions, and decide whether the wave should continue, split, or close
- **Closure** — mark the disposition of all wave changes, produce the next-wave handoff, and update journals and promotion candidates

### Implement Loop Execution Model

The coordinator's execution loop during the implement phase follows a ReAct-derived model — explicit Reasoning, Action, and Observation at every lane boundary. Key properties:

- **Thought before action:** the coordinator records a `Thought:` entry in the Progress Log before each lane invocation, stating why this action now.
- **Wave plan:** before the first edit, the coordinator produces an ordered lane sequence with scoped inputs per serialization unit; deviations are named events, not silent reorderings.
- **Parallel lane merge:** implementation and computational-verification lanes with no shared dependencies run concurrently; routine inferential reviewer lanes run later in the distinct `Review wave` phase.
- **Finding classification (CRITIC):** after an exceptional named checkpoint or the delivery review, findings are evaluated against the change doc's acceptance criteria before a loop level is chosen — "reviewer clean" alone is not the exit condition.
- **Root cause capture (Reflexion):** after a blocking finding, the coordinator records a `Reflect:` entry identifying the pattern and updating remaining tasks proacti

vely.
- **Three loop levels:** Level 1 (micro — internal to implementer, no log entry), Level 2 (exceptional focused independent checkpoint — re-check the affected boundary, no re-Prepare), Level 3 (wave lifecycle — scope or plan invalidation, stop and re-Prepare or re-plan). Finding type — not severity — determines the level.

See `001-framework-lifecycle-overview.md` section 3a for the full loop model, finding classification table, and escalation reference.

### Wave Artifact Contract

Wave artifacts should be machine-usable without becoming rigid fill-in-the-blank templates. The goal is to preserve stable anchors and relationship semantics so other agents can read, continue, challenge, and reconcile the wave reliably.

Each wave artifact must expose stable identifiers and state anchors sufficient to recover operational, coordination, assumption, disposition, and handoff truth, such as:

- `Change ID`
- `wave-id`
- `Status`
- `Coordinator`
- `Objective`
- `Participants`
- `Changes`
- `Dependencies`
- `Assumptions`
- `Review Checkpoints`
- `Journal Refs`
- `Next-Wave Handoff`

For machine usability, each wave should make these relationships explicit when they exist:

- which participants own or review which changes or tasks
- which changes depend on which other changes
- which assumptions are frozen, tentative, invalidated, or newly discovered
- which review checkpoints gate progress or closure
- which incomplete changes or tasks were deferred, moved, retried, blocked, or superseded

Changes should support variable depth while preserving stable anchors. A change may be atomic or composite, and optional tasks/subtasks may be tracked inside the change document when finer execution state is useful. A normal wave record should expose:

- `Change ID`
- `Change Status`
- optional `Previous Change Status`
- title or scope
- owner
- dependencies
- expected outputs
- review requirements
- blockers or risks
- child tasks, subtasks, or workstreams when the change is composite

Wave artifacts should also preserve time-sequenced operational state when useful, for example:

- coordinator decisions
- new findings
- invalidated assumptions
- review outcomes
- state transitions for changes or tasks

This does not require a rigid event log template, but it does require enough explicit state that another agent can reconstruct what happened and why the wave is in its current condition.

### Change Carry-Forward Policy

Waves are operational containers. Changes are the durable units of scope and intent tracked inside waves.

- a wave may contain one or more changes
- a change may appear in more than one wave
- a wave should close even when some change work remains incomplete, as long as the disposition of that remaining work is explicit

Default policy:

- when a change is not finished at wave closure, keep the same `Change ID` and carry its unfinished work into a later wave
- move, defer, retry, or rescope the unfinished change work explicitly rather than inventing a new change identifier by default

Split a change into a new change only when:

- the remaining work has become materially different in purpose or scope
- the unfinished work now needs separate planning, review, or decision treatment
- the original change is effectively complete and the remainder is follow-on work rather than continuation
- keeping the same `Change ID` would hide a real shift in intent, risk, or accountability

## Persona Model

Persona agents represent the **users, operators, administrators, and deployers** of the software system being built — not the agents who build it. They are invoked to give the user perspective during spec authoring, design review, and acceptance.

- personas are distinct from agent roles: roles build the software; personas speak as the people who use or operate it
- persona creation should be evidence-driven; do not invent personas for style or symmetry
- ground each persona in usage patterns, behavior contracts, and user-facing failure modes

found in the project (from evidence in the repository)
- when evidence is sparse, ask the user who operates or uses the system before generating persona docs
- persona count should stay justified by evidence; start small and expand only when a meaningfully distinct usage pattern requires it
- personas participate in spec authoring, design review, edge-case analysis, and acceptance — not in implementation or coordination

Factor-review agents are a separate concern from user personas. See the `## Factor Review Model` section below.

## Factor Review Model

Factor review agents are specialized AI reviewer subagents that evaluate a wave's changes against one specific operational concern. They complement — not replace — the generic `architecture-reviewer`, `security-reviewer`, and `performance-reviewer` roles.

The canonical reference is the 15-factor model: the original Twelve-Factor App methodology plus three IBM extensions. Factor review is not limited to cloud-native services — individual factors apply whenever the project evidence supports them.

**Threshold for creating a factor-review agent:** a factor warrants a dedicated subagent when it introduces at least 2–3 concrete review questions that the generic reviewer roles would not naturally ask. If a factor overlaps entirely with an existing reviewer's scope, skip it.

**Implementation:** generate a `.claude/agents/factor-<nn>-<name>.md` file for each applicable factor (zero-padded number keeps directory listings sorted). Each agent file should describe: what this factor means, what evidence in this project makes it relevant, what questions it asks when reviewing a wave, and whether its findings are gating or advisory for this project.

### The 15 Factors and Applicability Signals

| # | Factor | Create a review agent when |
|---|---|---|
| 01 | **Codebase** | Project has multiple deploy targets, environment-per-branch patterns, or a monorepo with shared app code |
| 02 | **Dependencies** | Project uses a package

manager with declared dependencies and isolation requirements |
| 03 | **Config** | Project reads configuration values that differ by environment, user, or deployment context |
| 04 | **Backing services** | Project connects to external services — databases, caches, IoT bridges, APIs, message brokers — as attached resources |
| 05 | **Build / release / run** | Project has a formal build pipeline, distributable artifact, or CI/CD with strictly separated build and run stages |
| 06 | **Processes** | Project is designed to run as stateless processes with explicit scaling or worker-pool requirements |
| 07 | **Port binding** | Project binds to a network port or exposes an HTTP, gRPC, or WebSocket interface |
| 08 | **Concurrency** | Project is designed to scale by adding concurrent instances or workers |
| 09 | **Disposability** | Project runs as a daemon, service, or long-running process with graceful startup and shutdown requirements |
| 10 | **Dev / prod parity** | Project has meaningfully distinct development, staging, and production environments |
| 11 | **Logs** | Project has structured logging, event-stream observability, or operational output contracts |
| 12 | **Admin processes** | Project has CLI tools, one-off operational commands, or management scripts run alongside the main process |
| 13 | **API first** *(IBM)* | Project exposes an API as a first-class integration contract consumed by other systems or services |
| 14 | **Telemetry** *(IBM)* | Project has monitoring, alerting, distributed tracing, or operational dashboard requirements |
| 15 | **Auth and security** *(IBM)* | Project has authentication, authorization, multi-user access control, or externally-facing trust boundaries |

**When to skip a factor:** if the project provides no concrete evidence for the applicability signal, record the factor as `not-applicable` with a one-line rationale in `docs/repo-profile.json` under `factor_review`. Do not generate an agent file for skipped factors. Re-evaluat

e skipped factors during **`Upgrade Wavefoundry`** (legacy: **`Upgrade wave framework`** / **`Upgrade wave context`**) when project scope changes.

**Relation to generic reviewers:** factor agents are narrow specialists. They ask factor-specific questions that the general reviewer pool would otherwise miss. When a factor overlaps closely with an existing reviewer (e.g., factor 15 auth/security overlaps with `security-reviewer`), keep both but define non-overlapping scope in each agent's instructions.

## Journal Model

Journals are structured episodic memory for roles and personas.

- journals are advisory, not source of truth
- repeated, validated lessons can be promoted
- journals should stay bounded over time through distillation, archival, and retention policy rather than unbounded accumulation
- promotion targets include repo-local workflow memory, prompt docs, persona docs, or canonical docs

## Migration Model

Older non-wave context footprints should be treated as legacy source material during migration.

- `160-upgrade-wavefoundry.prompt.md` should be able to initialize missing wave-context artifacts in repos that already use the legacy framework
- `220-legacy-framework-migration.prompt.md` defines the migration helper behavior
- delete the legacy framework only after the migration path is validated

**When the permissions block first appears, and who can trigger the render.** A fresh install and a protocol-bridge upgrade render the permissions block immediately. An ordinary upgrade of an existing target also renders it during that same upgrade, but only because of deliberate backstops in the upgrade's later phases: the in-process orchestrator that runs the surface-rendering phase is pre-extraction code, so on the transition upgrade that phase runs the OLD renderer, which has no permissions switch. The backstops run only from phases the upgrade executes in a SEPARATE process on the freshly extracted code, which is what closes that old-code window. The cleanup phase carries the site every upgrade path reaches (`wf upgrade --cleanup` on the CLI, `wf_upgrade(phase="cleanup")` through MCP); the index-refresh phase carries a second one for the flows that run it. Without them the block would first appear one full upgrade cycle later. Rendering is **operator-approved rather than structurally unreachable by an agent**: `wf_upgrade` is an ordinary agent-callable tool and its first phase renders, so an agent can trigger the render, but only at the **read tier**, because the write tier needs the operator knob and `wf_upgrade` is itself a write-tier tool and so cannot allowlist itself. Likewise, the knob living in `.claude/sett

If the committed `.claude/settings.json` already carried those allow rules by hand, the render claims nothing, the provenance stays empty, and those rules get no rename self-heal; the consent output reports them as already present and left unmanaged. **Upgrade REPORTING no longer waits a cycle (and what still does).** The same old-code window used to apply to the upgrade's own reporting: the primary-phase summary sentinel was built by the pre-extraction orchestrator, so any change to what the upgrade reports shipped one upgrade late and produced false "the fix does not work" field reports. Three class boundaries matter when reading upgrade output: (a) sentinel-carried summary fields take effect on the upgrade that installs them; (b) behavior-class fixes (what the upgrade DOES mid-run) still need a pack hook bridge, like the permissions backstops above, to act on their installing upgrade; and (c) server-resident response fields (`runner_stale`, diagnostics composition,

response bounding) are computed by the running MCP server and still require a full host restart on every release. One residual fires exactly once per target: the upgrade that first installs the delegation is still driven by a pre-delegation parent, so that single transition run reports an old-schema summary. Do not report that one transition run's old-schema summary as the backstop failing to work; every later upgrade reports on fresh code.

If that install fails (offline, proxy or TLS interception, application control), the index update does not run: the summary's `index_update` reads `not run: dependency provisioning failed; run wf setup` (the recommended command is `wf setup`), `dependency_provisioning_failed` is `true`, and `wf_upgrade` returns a `dependency_provisioning_failed` diagnostic instead of an index publication failure. The cleanup summary carries `setup_status` (`ready`, `action_required`, `indeterminate` or `not_assessed`), `setup_reasons` and `setup_command`; when cleanup does not record a new setup baseline (the prior one describes another environment, or the index or dependency step failed), these report the assessment against the baseline left in place, which is what later readiness checks report, so the summary never says `ready` while they say otherwise. When setup is not ready after cleanup, `next_step` recommends `setup_command` ahead of `wf_reload_mcp` (report it to the operator and ask before running it). Transition runs: the setup fields come from the new-code `--cleanup` process, so they appear on the upgrade that installs them. The separate dependency step changes what Phase 4 does, and on the default path of both `wf upgrade` and `wf_upgrade()` Phase 4 runs in the pre-extraction orchestrator, so it takes effect from the next upgrade (it applies at once when Phase 4 runs as a new-code process: `--

update-index`, `--rebuild-index`); that transition run still installs through the Phase 4 child's own dependency check, and if that install fails the upgrade completes but reports an index publication failure recommending `index_build`. On that run, follow the cleanup summary's `setup_command` (`wf setup`) instead: `index_build` cannot install a missing package. The new `next_step` is computed by the running server, so it appears after `wf_reload_mcp` or a restart onto the new code. Do not report either transition run as the fix failing.

**Reading token presence (do this before reporting a missing token).** `summary_schema_version` is NOT delegation-exclusive: the cleanup phase's emit site carries it too, on both the success and the failure branch. Present, it says only that post-extraction framework code rendered THIS summary; it never says which emitter produced it, and it never claims the upgrade succeeded (`failed_phase` is the success discriminator). Absent, it has three distinct causes and a field report must name which one applies instead of reporting a bare "absent":

1. **The in-process degradation fallback produced the summary.** Always accompanied by `summary_source_degraded`, which names the delegation failure class.
2. **The runner predates this contract.** Distinguished by `to_version`.
3. **No summary was emitted at all.** An interrupted phase can emit no sentinel; inspect its retained failure state and follow the matching recovery before cleanup.

"A sentinel was emitted without the token" and "no sentinel was emitted" are different observations with different causes. Report them as different observations; collapsing both into one "absent" reading is the reporting half of the defect this contract exists to remove.

When the installed revision predates **1.5.0**, `upgrade_extensions.post_extract` runs three migrations automatically at the `post_extract` phase boundary (immediately after zip extraction, before surface rendering). The operator does not invoke them; the upgrade machinery fires them inside the standard `Upgrade Wavefoundry` flow. Each migration is idempotent — re-running the upgrade is safe.

The migrations:

1. **`Role:` backfill on every `docs/agents/*.md`** — wave `1p35d` (`1p35l`) made `docs-lint` enforce `Role:` on every agent role doc. Existing repos may have custom agent docs added since their last install that lack this field; without the backfill, the first post-upgrade docs gate run fails. The migration walks `docs/agents/`, `docs/agents/specialists/`, `docs/agents/personas/` (skipping `README.md`, `session-handoff.md`, `platform-mapping.md`, and anything under `journals/`) and inserts `Role: <filename-slug>` into any file missing the field. The `Role:` is placed immediately after the `Status:` line (or after `Owner:` if `Status:` is absent).
2. **Pycache launcher cleanup** — wave `1p35d` (`1p35n`) retired the `pycache-cleanup` Claude Code hook. The migration deletes `.claude/hooks/pycache-cleanup`, `.claude/hooks/pycache-cleanup.py`, and `.claude/hooks/pycache-cleanup.cmd` if any remain.

When `wf_reload_mcp()` detects that a tool was added or removed, or that any tool's docstring changed between the pre-reload and post-reload snapshots, it dispatches the MCP `notifications/tools/list_changed` protocol notification to the connected client. The response reports server-side dispatch separately from client adoption; it cannot prove that the client refreshed its catalog. The response carries:

The old boolean response field `tool_list_changed_notification_sent`, the `queued` dispatch value, and the `tool_list_changed_notification_queued` diagnostic are retired.

The MCP protocol primitive is the standard re-fetch trigger, but adoption remains host-implementation-dependent and is not observable from the reload response.

An in-process implementation reload can still succeed in that case, but only a full host restart guarantees runner-file changes are loaded. A

he shared by every repository on

- Read the pack's mandatory `upgrade_protocol_version` and `minimum_runner_protocol` before extraction. Protocol 2 accepts only supported, non-decreasing integer metadata and returns `upgrade_protocol_invalid` for missing, malformed, unknown, or mismatched values.
- A protocol-1 runner must not extract a protocol-2 feature pack. Protocol-1 installations at version 1.8.0 or later upgrade directly with the same single matching `wavefoundry-<version>.zip` release package; do not install 1.14 as an intermediate step. A source below 1.8.0 stops before mutation and must first be upgraded to the supported floor. The agent first stops the Wavefoundry dashboard, disconnects/stops every Wavefoundry MCP server for this repository, and leaves the current host session idle; it then runs the response's exact `command_argv` through its ordinary non-MCP shell (equivalent to `python <package>.zip --root <repo> --confirm-hosts-stopped`). No operator-entered terminal command is required. The package verifies both embedded hashes, acquires lifecycle then publication/dashboard locks, atomically swaps only `.wavefoundry/framework/` with rollbac

k retained, proves the installed runner is protocol 2, and immediately executes the exact hash-bound feature hop. After the package finishes or pauses, fully restart every attached host before any lifecycle mutation and follow its bounded structured recovery result. An already-loaded protocol-1 MCP wrapper predates the 1.15 response cap and cannot be retrofitted by the incoming pack; its compact bridge JSON is emitted last. If the host truncates or rejects that one legacy response, the agent — not the operator — uses its ordinary shell to detect the single installed package and run the same package/root/confirmation entry point after Wavefoundry services stop. A bridge is not a product release and may not contain or write project surfaces; there is no special upgrade package, and the normal structured `command_argv` remains authoritative whenever the host returns it.
- Protocol-2 Upgrade preflights config, every registered lifecycle carrier, and every non-closed declared wave before the first project write. It maps legacy enabled review to `enabled=true, delivery_mode=targeted` and disabled review to `enabled=false, delivery_mode=disabled`, replaces only recognized lifecycle sections, marks/reprojects non-closed declared waves for re-Prepare when the migration changes the policy (a no-op migration marks nothing and rewrites no wave), and never rewrites closed waves or prior event records. Ambiguous carriers fail with an actionable path and no writes.
- Upgrade holds the shared strict lifecycle lock before the publication lock for each process-bounded transaction. The fsynced JSON checkpoint is recovery state, not a lock. An interrupted process releases both locks; continuation reacquires them in the same order and repeats the appropriate preflight. Every other registered publisher fails fast with `upgrade_in_progress` until terminal cleanup.
- Council signoff keys: from this release new approvals are written as `council-readiness` and `council-delivery`. The earlier

`wave-council-*` spellings stay valid in workflow configs, as `wf_review_event` input and in recorded history, and every reader accepts both, so no config, wave record or `events.jsonl` ledger needs rewriting.

- This upgrades the project's Wave Framework layer in the repository to the framework version currently available at `.wavefoundry/framework/` **after** step 0 when step 0 unpacks a root distribution zip, whether or not that version has been committed yet.
- It does not fetch a newer framework release on its own (step 0 only unpacks zips already present at the repository root).
- Step 0 is never a terminal success condition by itself; unpacking without the subsequent reconciliation and verification steps is an incomplete upgrade.

# 179 - Envision Project

**Applicable when:** any project. Establish or revise an ambitious product vision and an adaptive roadmap through useful, enduring capabilities and their technical and nontechnical prerequisites. This is an authoring workflow, not implementation planning or autonomous execution.

**Shortcut:** `Envision project` · **Skill:** `wf-envision`

Imagine what this product could make possible for people and why that future matters. Seek the greatest relevant value, financial and otherwise, while making tradeoffs and uncertainty visible. The vision names the desired future; supporting strategy explains the choices and path from today's reality. A roadmap of technical and nontechnical advances makes that path credible. Selecting the next investment follows from this argument.

## Scope and output

Default output is `VISION.md` at the repository root; a new document is titled `<Project>: Vision and Roadmap`. Preserve existing titles and canonical locations unless the operator requests a change, and honor requested filenames. Preserve valid existing material and unrelated operator edits. When reopening an early or provisional vision, retain worthwhile ambition as an explicit option unless the operator rejected it; permission to revise does not mean permission to shrink. Synthesize newly clarified uses and beneficiaries into the product purpose and explain directional changes. Detailed review evidence belongs in a sibling such as `VISION-review.md`, or the existing canonical review location; honor response-only evidence requests. A discussion, prompt-writing request or explicit read-only review writes neither artifact: return the requested advice and review record in the conversation.

For a new or substantially revised vision, default to advisory coverage of product strategy, the domain or application workflow, senior architecture and independent challenge. A substantial revision changes purpose, beneficiary, the set of horizons or their order; other e

dits use affected reviews proportionately. Select scope and depth by stakes, maturity and uncertainty, adding relevant expertise where consequential. Narrowing the default requires a stated reason tied to that brief, never lower author effort alone; high-stakes or highly uncertain visions keep the default unless the operator directs otherwise. Honor explicit review requests and operator-directed changes, narrowing or omission. These are advisory artifact reviews, not lifecycle gates. This workflow creates no wave, implementation backlog, deployment, commit or publication, and grants no implementation or approval authority.

## 1. Establish the brief

Reuse the conversation, existing vision and project context. Establish the intended ambition, beneficiary, outcome, planning horizon, constraints and deliverable. Use an adaptive interview only for material gaps: who struggles and what progress they seek; what they do or use today; the team's pivotal insight; why now; whom and what the product will deliberately not serve; who adopts, pays for or sustains it and why; and what failure would look like even if it ships. Do not turn this question bank into a mandatory questionnaire.

When material information is missing, combine necessary questions and your inferred-brief readback in one pre-draft exchange. Keep the questions brief and separate them from the review notice in readable paragraphs. With a sufficient brief, state the interpretation and proceed without seeking confirmation. Defer nonblocking questions into the draft; explain the consequence of genuinely blocking strategic ambiguity.

In that same briefing, state selected review roles, any additional expertise, reason for narrowing and expected effort. Do not separately ask approval for the readback or routine reviews: the notice lets the operator steer. The default has four reviewer responsibilities; use separate independent contexts for selected roles, or disclose shared context and missing independence. No addi

tional chair or consensus process is required. Apply the stakes rule rather than assigning every specialty to every product. Distinguish selected scope from actual concurrency or host reuse; invent no cost or duration estimates. Reuse an already explicit scope without another interruption.

A twelve-month horizon and unlimited resources are optional parameters, not defaults. Do not impose autonomous agents, cloud services, a business model or a fixed number of horizons. Use only this project's brief and sources.

## 2. Ground the need and starting point

Build a compact diagnosis: the progress beneficiaries seek in their circumstances, what makes it hard, the insight that opens a better possibility and why the opportunity is timely. Use supplied interviews, observations, usage/support evidence or research. Distinguish sourced observations, interpretations and untested hypotheses. An enduring need or provisional timing hypothesis is legitimate; invented urgency, customers or testimony is not. Repository facts establish capability, not demand. Missing primary research permits a provisional vision with visible gaps; identify the cheapest useful research into the most consequential uncertain need. Neither a fixed interview count nor this workflow substitutes for primary research or stakeholder alignment.

Follow the target repository's instructions and investigation workflow. Where Wavefoundry retrieval is configured for that target, use Guru and indexed retrieval, then validate load-bearing claims against current source. Confirm a delegated worker's actual tool access. If target-scoped MCP retrieval is unavailable, use targeted local inspection and disclose the evidence gap; an index attached to a different repository is not evidence for this target.

Inspect the existing vision, project orientation, architecture, operating constraints and implementation relevant to the direction. Before recommending work, distinguish capabilities already working, working with limitati

ons, genuinely missing and not yet established, using current source, operating artifacts and operator experience. Attribute reported success and its scope separately from independently reproduced behavior; lack of broad evaluation does not mean a working capability is absent. Treat demonstrated strengths as foundations to preserve or extend, not features to recreate. Resolve consequential contradictions or retain them as uncertainty. Use focused safe checks where an executable claim matters; historical plans, record validation and confident prose alone do not prove shipped behavior. Do not repeat installation inventories, broad audits, unrelated suites, setup or environment changes without a decision-relevant reason.

Research consequential choices using relevant available products, approaches and industry practices, including what has worked, what has failed and under which conditions. Reuse adequate supplied or recent research; scale further investigation to stakes, uncertainty and the decisions it could change. Record sources and dates, distinguish vendor claims, practitioner accounts and comparative evidence, and explain limitations and implications for this product. Public research is not customer validation, and one success or failure is not a universal result. Use external research only within the operator's authorized scope; disclose missing or stale evidence and the question it leaves open, or request needed access. Do not silently add network research to a local-only engagement or fabricate a landscape. Keep decision-relevant conclusions in the vision; substantial source detail may live in a sibling research file, preserving existing material and response-only boundaries.

Identify tensions between the destination and today's architecture or product boundary. Explain the transition and future decision needed; neither silently change today's contract nor treat it as an eternal limit on ambition.

## 3. Draft the vision and roadmap

Lead with a short, repea

table destination statement in the beneficiary's language: what becomes possible and why it matters. Follow it with a concise roadmap overview before detailed rationale. The opening alone should convey the distinctive future; the roadmap explains how useful stages make it real. Write a coherent argument, not a feature wishlist or completed headings.

Keep three things legible without forcing three headings: the transformative product capacity sought, unresolved breakthroughs or research bets, and the useful stages toward it. Describe future capacity as aspiration, not established capability or a guaranteed result. Missing present proof is not disproof of an ambitious destination; evidence calibrates current claims, uncertain bets and the route. Preserve genuine contrary evidence and its consequences. A proposed reduction in destination is an operator-owned strategic choice, not a factual correction. A small first advance must support or test the larger future, never silently replace it.

Scale depth to stakes, maturity and uncertainty, with no fixed word ceiling. Diagnosis, strategic choices and non-goals, foundations, useful horizons, consequential dependencies, riskiest assumptions and the next bounded advance remain core. Add analytical detail only when it helps a consequential choice or makes the path credible; a small internal tool or library need not carry a competitor study or elaborate measurement machinery.

### Destination and strategic choices

When the destination is open, explore meaningfully different futures and recommend one with reasons. When the operator has chosen it, preserve it. Do not limit the future to an extrapolation of today's implementation or backlog. Make the destination memorable through a concrete end-to-end experience: what people do, what the system does, where human judgment remains and what people receive. Connect the diagnosis and pivotal insight to this experience. Explain financial and nonfinancial value, costs and beneficiary

tradeoffs without inventing a common score or asserting that one direction is provably optimal.

Compare real alternatives where consequential, including existing manual practice, competing products, do-it-yourself or doing nothing. Explain who/where to focus, why people would choose this product, and deliberate non-goals and sacrifices. Use advantage analysis when it helps explain a choice; distinguish a benefit from the mechanism that could sustain its value. Label unproven claims; do not invent a moat. For internal, public or open products, enduring usefulness, adoption and stewardship may matter more than excluding competitors.

### From the destination to useful horizons

Work backward from the ultimate experience to necessary capabilities, foundations and prerequisites, then forward through useful horizons. Cite current capabilities concisely, including their verification limits and the distance to the destination. If source and documentation conflict, explain the consequence for the path. Label proposals and unresolved research.

Assess value, usability, feasibility and viability at the destination. Each horizon needs a beneficiary outcome, useful intermediate value if later horizons never arrive, and meaningful conditions for advancing or reconsidering. Identify which consequential risk it reduces and what evidence will resolve it. Near horizons have concrete end-to-end demonstrations, exit criteria and failure conditions; an unchanged baseline must fail a new capability demonstration. Detail and precision decrease with distance: later horizons state intended outcomes, consequential assumptions, provisional advancement/reconsideration conditions and evidence needed to firm them up. Qualitative conditions are valid. Do not invent distant numerical targets, dates or implementation commitments; retain justified operator-supplied timing as an explicit aspiration or constraint. Where research must precede a usable slice, name its uncertainty, stopping condition a

nd the beneficiary value it enables; research activity or infrastructure completion alone is not product value.

Treat relevant nontechnical work as roadmap work alongside engineering: research, adoption, distribution, funding, partnerships, operating practices and team capability may have milestones and prerequisites. Include only tracks the product needs, connecting each to an outcome or uncertainty it resolves. Explain cross-workstream dependencies, including where a nontechnical prerequisite gates an engineering advance; count these dependencies toward the critical path, not as a disconnected checklist.

Explain how each advance enables what follows. Include components, state ownership, interfaces, instrumentation and uncertainties where they explain the path. Show dependencies, parallel opportunities, critical path and timing assumptions; exit evidence establishes completion. If unlimited-resource analysis helps the argument, explain what extra experiments or specialists buy and which bottlenecks remain; more workers do not imply proportional progress. Keep detailed tickets outside the vision.

Consider architecture, security, modernization, reliability and performance alongside product and nontechnical advances when they enable the destination or remove a consequential constraint. Connect each proposed improvement to beneficiary value and a horizon; do not force an item from every category or turn vision authoring into a whole-project audit.

### Endurance and adaptation

Explain how the product remains operable and changeable, at the depth its risks warrant. Distinguish durable principles from current rules proposed for reconsideration. Name consequential sources of truth, ownership/contracts, trust boundaries, execution locations and integrations; use a component/data-flow diagram when it clarifies existing and proposed foundations. Address maintenance, feedback, human decisions, costly-to-reverse commitments, replaceable boundaries and migration where relev

ant. Keep unresolved designs visible and preserve justified options without speculative extensibility.

For a major assumption that could fail, explain what remains useful, what would change and which decision returns to the operator. Revisit the vision when horizons meet or miss exit criteria, critical assumptions or questions change, or new beneficiary/market evidence changes the brief. Adaptation should preserve the purpose where justified while making any proposed change of destination explicit.

For substantial technical shifts, separate reported burden from established cause. Use relevant workload, latency, memory, failure, deployment and maintenance evidence to compare retaining or tuning the current design, targeted replacement or integration, and broader migration where credible. Assess compatibility, support, operational complexity, migration cost and a useful incremental path. A technology change does not by itself establish an improvement; tie expected benefits to the target project's constraints and evidence. Recommend a discriminating benchmark or prototype when evidence is insufficient, or a bounded migration when supported; neither presume a rewrite nor rule out ambitious change.

### Evidence and immediate next steps

State how success and failure would be recognized, proportionate to the claim. Where measurement helps, propose a primary beneficiary outcome metric with guardrails against harm or gaming, or a small justified set if one number would distort the purpose. Explain necessary baselines, observation windows and limits; do not force a detailed evaluation design onto a claim that needs a simpler demonstration. Include reliability, total cost, maintenance burden, failures, abandonment, human rescues and delayed regressions where relevant. Distinguish targets and proposed metrics from observed results; activity counts are not success measures.

Map the riskiest assumptions to cheap discriminating experiments and the evidence that would change t

he decision. Use independent evaluation, repeated attempts and held-out cases when the credibility of the claim needs them, whether or not the product is agentic. For agentic systems, specifically assess evidence quality and separation of evaluator from evaluated system. State what cannot yet be justified, simulated, measured or guaranteed.

End the roadmap argument with a concise, ordered set of immediate advances that connect the ultimate demonstration and nearer horizons to action. For each, explain the observed problem or opportunity, current capability, useful incremental outcome, why it comes now, consequential dependencies and evidence for continuing or reconsidering. Distinguish preserving, extending, investigating or validating, and building capabilities; missing evidence may justify validation rather than rebuilding. Include enabling technical work where justified, and choose a useful number of priorities rather than a fixed quota. Keep this a synthesis of the vision's reasoning, not a duplicate backlog or automatic implementation plan.

An optional clarity check is a short fictional future announcement and three hard customer FAQ questions. Keep it temporary unless requested, label it as imagined and never invent real testimony. This tests narrative clarity, not customer validation.

## 4. Review one identified draft

The author coordinates review but does not impersonate independent reviewers. Give each worker the same identified draft (path and revision or content fingerprint), brief, evidence sources, write boundaries and relevant unresolved questions. Reviewer work is read-only against source and the vision. Parallel independent reads are useful; serialize revisions so reviewers know which draft they judged.

Give reviewers the reader outcome test in section 3. Preserve the requested ambition across every review and repair. Correct false capability claims, broken reasoning, unsupported certainty and dependency errors. Challenges to the destination's s

ize or direction are explicit strategic decisions for the operator, not permission to silently substitute a safer or smaller future. Keep contrary feasibility evidence, consequences and alternatives visible; distinguish desired outcomes, assumptions and established facts. Continue reviews under the established scope without another routine approval; return only for material scope/authority changes or unresolved strategic choices.

Assign concrete reviewer responsibilities, using applicable project role instructions where present and the remits below otherwise. These are analytical assignments, not claims of professional credentials, stakeholder representation or customer validation. Each reviewer grounds findings in the identified brief and evidence, names limitations, and separates observations from hypotheses. Assigning a role does not require enabling one in configuration or installing anything.

| Default responsibility | Outcome and evidence to examine |
| --- | --- |
| Product strategy | Distinctive beneficiary value, transformative destination, strategic choices and sacrifices, real alternatives, adoption and viability. Test whether immediate priorities advance the ultimate purpose. |
| Domain or application workflow | End-to-end fit with actual work, obligations, constraints and adoption. Distinguish observed needs and operating experience from imagined workflows; identify missing domain or customer evidence. |
| Senior architecture | Current-state accuracy, unsolved breakthroughs versus engineering foundations, dependency order, ownership, interfaces, trust boundaries, feasible transition and adaptability. |
| Independent challenge | Failure modes, unsupported certainty, contrary evidence and stronger alternatives. Challenge the argument without silently shrinking the operator's ambition. |

Add finance/economics when funding, cost to serve or sustainability shapes the choice; security when trust or authority is consequential; reliability when operation and

recovery determine value; and UX when interaction uncertainty needs dedicated scrutiny. Explain the selected coverage and consequential omissions. Labels and review counts are not evidence that these questions were answered.

For architecture, use `docs/agents/architecture-reviewer.md` or the project's actual role, with seed `214-architecture-reviewer.prompt.md` as fallback. For independent challenge, use the canonical standalone Red-team review (`docs/prompts/red-team-review.prompt.md` and `docs/agents/specialists/red-team.md`; fallback seeds `177-red-team-review.prompt.md` and `225-red-team.prompt.md`), choose an appropriate lens and retain its required output. Follow applicable independence and execution protocols, reporting actual shared context, unavailable coverage and author self-checks honestly.

Archetypes may be optional thinking techniques within a review; they do not create a five-seat roster, chair or consensus requirement for Envision. When the operator explicitly requests a standalone Archetype Council, follow `docs/prompts/archetype-council.prompt.md`, full seed `236-archetype-council.prompt.md`, and its chair instructions. Report that selected form and actual execution separately; do not call informal use of a stance a completed Council. Proportionate scope does not relax a selected form's protocol. The author synthesizes evidence, improvements and open decisions; neither majority opinion nor consensus substitutes for an operator-owned strategic choice.

**Artifact-only boundary:** instructions about delivery-wave records in generic role documents apply when performing that lifecycle. Here, do not call Prepare, Review wave or review-approval tools, create wave records or write `council-readiness`/`council-delivery` approvals. A vision review does not replace required specialist or Wave Council approval for later implementation. Credible security issues go to the appropriate specialist; red-team does not issue security signoffs.

**Capability limit:

** if independent workers, required instructions or a review capability are unavailable, continue useful authorized drafting or advice. Label any author self-check as such, identify the missing review and leave that outcome pending. Never claim it passed, silently relabel the author as a reviewer, or reconfigure the host to make it available. If a review is explicitly omitted by the operator, record that scope without pretending it ran. A draft with pending review remains usable but is not described as independently reviewed in those areas.

## 5. Reconcile, validate and deliver

Collect initial findings before editing. Apply canonical dispositions, explain material decisions and incorporate accepted improvements into the argument. Preserve genuine research uncertainty and operator-owned strategic choices as open questions. When revising an existing vision, preserve unrelated material, reconcile contradictions and explain substantive directional changes.

Use one initial review pass, one bounded author repair pass and one focused verification by affected reviewers. At that boundary, report remaining actionable findings and decisions rather than starting an automatic review loop or claiming convergence. A material change of direction may need a new brief and review scope; obtain that decision before proceeding with dependent work.

Put draft identity, selected and executed roles, any optional forms/axes, findings or verdicts, material dispositions, incorporated changes, open operator decisions and unavailable/omitted coverage in the sibling review file or selected evidence location. State context sharing and evidence limits; selected coverage is not completed coverage. Preserve existing sibling content rather than blindly overwriting it. Keep at most a short dated review-status link in the vision; enduring assumptions and strategic questions still belong in its argument. Keep routine reviewer transcripts temporary and retain evidence for material conclusions. Read-on

ly requests keep this record in the response and change no files.

Check citations, links, prerequisite order and the horizon content contract. Run applicable documentation validation: with target-scoped Wavefoundry MCP use `wf_validate_docs`; without it use the project's supported docs check (Wavefoundry CLI: POSIX `./.wavefoundry/bin/wf docs-lint`, native Windows `.\.wavefoundry\bin\wf.cmd docs-lint`). Fix introduced defects and report unrelated failures without widening scope. Passing docs lint proves document consistency, not that the future capabilities exist.

At delivery, state whether the project or operator has explicitly adopted the vision; authoring, review and Git tracking alone do not adopt it. If it is not adopted, explain how to designate it with a one-line pointer in `AGENTS.md` or the project overview, for example `Canonical product vision and roadmap: VISION.md`, using the actual path. Do not write a designation without operator direction; preserve existing adoption when revising a designated vision.

Once adopted, subsequent Plan change work identifies which horizon and outcome the requested change advances and carries forward consequential prerequisites and assumptions; it does not select work or redirect the request to manufacture alignment. A designated uncommitted vision counts; a committed draft does not. **Delivery evidence informs horizon progress; recording it in the vision is an Envision revision or an explicit operator edit.** Met or missed exit conditions inform reconsideration without silently changing the destination or authorizing subsequent work. Planning leaves vision and review artifacts unchanged, adds no tracker, mandatory section or vision prerequisite, and accepts legitimate changes without direct horizon fit.

Return the document path or requested read-only advice, central direction, value and horizon sequence, research and capability-validation limits, actual review outcome and material open decisions. Explain how the result

meets the brief, what the operator should inspect first, and what changed in direction and why. Summarize the ordered immediate advances and their connection to the vision without automatically creating plans or starting work.

## [1.39.0] - 2026-10-29

### Added

- Envision project / `wf-envision` defines an ambitious product vision and an adaptable long-horizon roadmap, with useful technical and nontechnical advances and proportionate advisory reviews. Its opening makes the destination clear; distant horizons retain advancement conditions without invented precision. Decision-relevant research and validation of existing capabilities ground ordered immediate advances, including enabling technical changes where justified; technical shifts require causal evidence and alternatives rather than assumed technology benefits. It distinguishes transformative destination, unresolved breakthroughs and useful stages without silently shrinking earlier ambition. Advisory coverage uses product strategy, domain/application workflow, senior architecture and independent challenge, with consequential specialties and optional archetype techniques or an explicitly requested Council. Plan change conditionally carries an explicitly adopted vision’s relevant outcomes and prerequisites without editing it. Seed 100 authors missing prompts; seed 160 guides changed-seed179 and seed170 reconciliation into existing prompts, preserving project additions and stopping conflicts. Subsequent rendering emits the skill for active hosts. Authoring grants no implementation authority. Waves 21u1e / 21tpc, 21tpp / 21vpo, 21y6d / 21xpg and 21xq1 / 21xq0; authoring evidence is case-specific, and the 21ux4 comparison did not establish superiority.

### Security

- Bound configuration, migration-prompt and gap-marker reads; reject unsafe file types and handle oversized or deeply nested input conservatively. Invalid download deadlines fall back per key without discarding valid neighboring settings. Wave 20gfk / 20gfg.
- Cap each retained child log at 1 MiB with an explicit elision marker and final diagnostic tail. Clean returned upgrade display text after raw protocol interpretation, preserving subprocess status and recovery decisions. Wave 20gx0 / 20gfh.

- `python3 -B`, `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE`, explicit read-only configuration and `WAVEFOUNDRY_DISABLE_BYTECODE_CACHE=1` disable project bytecode-cache reads and writes after configuration. The test runner respects those controls, and controlled read-only children remove an inherited cache prefix before startup. Direct external launches must unset `PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX` themselves; ordinary caching remains process-wide and source integrity checks do not authenticate cached bytecode. Wave 206fh / 206fi.
- Prompt and lifecycle-document moves, rollback cleanup, rendered-file removals and stale-launcher cleanup remove only the identity-checked source or newly published entry through its parent d

escriptor where supported. Changed or non-owned destinations are retained; the final identity-check/unlink sequence remains non-atomic. Wave 206fh / 207y4.
- `wf_map` excerpts and workflow-config reads use contained, bounded repository reads with an 8 MiB ceiling; linked leaf files and special files are refused with bounded fallback behavior. Wave 206fh / 207y5.

- Path and id containment for wave records, journals, vendored files and extension provenance. Change ids read from a wave record or passed to a lifecycle tool are now checked against one allow-list (`<prefix>-<kind> <slug>`) before any path is built from them. Member change documents are read only as regular files inside their own folder and inside the repository, through a size-capped read; staged plan listings and the dashboard apply the same rule, and docs-lint refuses a linked or non-regular member document in its wave-document check. On POSIX the upgrade's journal migration now creates and removes files only through directory handles reached by a no-follow walk, and its messages carry no absolute path. The offline vendored-script check reads only regular files confined to the vendor folder, under a size cap, and names a refused table row by its position rather than echoing it. `wf_server_info` extension paths are never absolute (`framework:` and `external:` labels). Bulk `wf_get_change` matches each member by its exact name instead of a substring. A wave-record member line whose id fails the allow-list is never read: the phase tools block with `change_id_invalid`, naming the record and line number; recover by editing that line by hand, then run `wf_validate_docs`. Behavior change: a wave folder that is a symbolic link resolving outside the repository no longer serves member change documents to the lifecycle tools; in-repository folder links keep working. Reported by the Waveforge maintainers. Wave 1zxo0 / 1zxns.
- Taking the lifecycle lock now refuses, and releases the lock again, when a reader in the

same process could release it through a link: the lock file has another hard link; a symlink or Windows junction resolves to a runtime lock anywhere in the record roots and archive, `docs/`, all of `.wavefoundry/` except a project-local `venv`, or the repository root's own entries; or a record-root directory link leads outside the repository. A link that names the checkout in another case, Unicode form or firmlink spelling is judged by file identity. The check opens no file, and an in-repository pnpm-style `node_modules` is not refused; it also refuses (`link_scan_limit`) when more than 50,000 entries are reachable only through directory links. The server reports `lifecycle_lock_link_refused` with the repository-relative link and its remedy, and `wf setup` and the upgrade runner report the same refusal instead of a busy lock. Found in review of wave 1zv87. Wave 1zv8c / 1zv8b.
- The upgrade's journal migration no longer follows links. A repository with retired journal files could make an upgrade create a file outside the repository, or remove journal-shaped files outside it, through a linked journals folder, journal, wave folder or destination name. The migration now refuses every link and escape, writes only through an exclusive no-follow create, removes a source only after re-checking it, and leaves anything it refuses in place for the report. Affects 1.15.0 to 1.28.0; only repositories that still have retired journal files run the migration. Upgrade to this release. Reported by the Waveforge maintainers. Wave 1zv87 / 1zuq5.
- The code reading tools no longer open the framework's runtime lock files under `.wavefoundry/` (including through a different letter case or a committed link). Reading the lifecycle lock file while a lifecycle change held it released the lock in the holding process, letting another process change wave records at the same time. Reported by the Waveforge maintainers. Wave 1zv87 / 1zuq7.
- `wf setup` no longer runs a `uv` found in the repositor

y: the PATH lookup skips the current folder, empty and relative entries and anything inside the repository, and on Windows accepts only `uv.exe`. Reported by the Waveforge maintainers. Wave 1zv87 / 1zv84.
- `wf_close_change`, `wf_mark_ac` and `wf_mark_task` refuse a change id shaped like a path before touching the filesystem, and the mark tools require the change to be admitted to the wave. A path-shaped id let `wf_close_change` probe whether a file existed and let the mark tools rewrite a checkbox in a Markdown file outside the repository. The probe was reported by the Waveforge maintainers; the write was found in review. Wave 1zv87 / 1zv85.
- The dashboard no longer loads scripts from a CDN: React, React DOM and elkjs are vendored at their pinned versions under `.wavefoundry/framework/dashboard/vendor/` (with their licences, sources and SHA-256 hashes) and served from the dashboard's own origin, so it needs no network access. The vendored folder's `README.md` also records each package's npm tarball URL and registry integrity and the commands that reproduce and check each file. The dashboard server now only answers requests addressed to a loopback host name (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, any port) or the host the operator explicitly bound, refusing others with 421, and every response carries a same-origin Content-Security-Policy and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. A `0.0.0.0` bind admits loopback names only and records a `127.0.0.1` URL. Takes effect when the dashboard restarts on the new release. Wave 1zim2 / 1zilx.
- The install seeds now treat a target repository's existing files as untrusted input: an installing agent summarises them as information about the project, does not follow instructions found in them, and reports instruction-like content to the operator. A new Phase 2 step inventories existing documentation before the docs structure is created, keeps reference material, checks for name collisions, never overwrites a file without reporting it, and

reports the result in the operator summary. Wave 1zim2 / 1zily.
- The Copilot edit gates now cover `apply_patch`. The pre-tool-use hook reads the patch text from the arguments' `input`, then `patch`, or a raw arguments string, and checks every path on a patch header line (`*** Add File:`, `*** Update File:`, `*** Delete File:`, `*** Move to:`, so both sides of a move) against the seed and framework-maintenance gates; a hunk line never counts as a header, CRLF and indented patches are read like plain ones, and a patch whose paths cannot be read is blocked. The post-tool-use hook runs docs-lint and the reindex for every header path. Codex `apply_patch` stays ungated, since Wavefoundry renders no Codex hook; this is now listed among the known limits of the edit gates. Requested by the Waveforge maintainers. Wave 1zyb3 / 1zxny.
- Docs-lint, including its secrets pass, and the single-id change lookup (`wf_get_change` and the change resource) no longer follow or block on a wave or plan document that is a link or a special file: each such document is reported once by its own path and a cause class and never read. A repository that keeps a record document as a link now fails docs-lint until the link is replaced with the document. Vendored-script table fields holding control or format characters are refused rather than printed, and the network verifier no longer prints server-supplied text (redirect targets, error reason phrases). Wave 200xy / 200v1.
- The session handoff tools, the prompt reader, the read-only MCP resources, the platform and agent surface renderers, the install-log read and prompt moves now read and write repository files through one contained primitive: a link leaving the repository or a special file is refused rather than followed or opened, reads are size-capped, file modes are set on the open file, and refusals name no path. Reported by the Waveforge maintainers. Wave 200ey / 1zyv2.
- Rendering agent surfaces now removes an undeclared skill or a retire

d skill file only when it is still the entry that was judged, render messages name repository-relative paths and exception classes only, file names printed by the moved-prompt link report have control and format characters escaped, and a deeply nested prompt-surface manifest is reported as unreadable instead of stopping the render. Reported by the Waveforge maintainers. Wave 200ey / 200eu.
- The journal migration preview no longer executes the distribution's declaration module; it reads the declaration statically. Upgrade extension helpers no longer leave the target's framework scripts directory on the module search path, and dry-run preview logs are never written through a link that leaves the repository. The review status now shows bracket characters in a self-attested approver name as replacement characters, so it cannot show a misleading handle; recorded approvals are unchanged. Reported by the Waveforge maintainers. Wave 200ey / 200ev.

- **The lifecycle and index-build locks can no longer be lost to an unrelated descriptor close, and `wf_reload_mcp` loads new `runtime_lock` code.** On POSIX these locks were classic record locks, which the kernel releases when the holding process closes any descriptor of the lock file, so lock safety depended on every in-process reader avoiding lock files. On Linux and

macOS (64-bit, x86_64 or arm64) they are now open file description (OFD) locks, which belong to the lock's own open file description; other platforms, and kernels or filesystems that reject OFD as unsupported, fall back to `lockf` as before. OFD and `lockf` locks exclude each other, so a process from an older release still running during an upgrade stays excluded. While another process holds an OFD index-build lock, `index_build_status` takes the owner pid from the lock metadata, because the kernel reports no pid for an OFD holder. As defense in depth for the fallback, the session handoff reader and writers, prompt lookup and the read-only resources refuse a target that resolves to a runtime lock without opening it (`runtime_lock_target_refused`, or a `# Refused` page); `wf_get_prompt` skips such a candidate and keeps searching. Separately, `wf_reload_mcp` failed with an import error when a release added a name to `runtime_lock`, because that module was never reloaded; it is now reloaded in place, keeping the in-process hold registry and its exception classes, and a test fails when a reloaded module imports a module the reload leaves stale without a recorded reason. A future release that changes a `runtime_lock` exception class definition will say that a host restart is needed. Native Windows is unchanged. Wave 1zxnz / 1zx02.
