## [1.28.0] - 2026-09-30

### Added

- **A distribution can serve Wavefoundry tools under its own names.** The extension declaration in `mcp_tool_extensions.py` gains `EXTENSION_TOOL_ALIASES` (extra served names), `EXTENSION_HIDDEN_TOOLS` (canonical names that are not served) and `EXTENSION_REPLACEMENTS` (a core name reused by an extension handler with a different schema, with the core behaviour kept under another name). An alias is a copy of the tool as served, so the lifecycle lock, the upgrade publication guard and cost accounting keyed on the canonical name apply to it. The core behaviour of a replaced name is wrapped separately under the core name, and the replacing handler neither triggers the core's argument-parsing extractors nor has its own hints rewritten. `next_tools`, `usage` and diagnostic recovery hints name the served tools; prose keeps canonical names, and `wf_server_info` publishes the canonical-to-served map. The permission allowlist includes aliases at their tier and omits hidden names. An invalid declaration refuses startup and leaves only runner tools served. The shipped declarations are empty and change nothing. Wave `1z8oz`.
- **Record vocabulary profiles.** What the record markers are called now lives in one place, the new `vocabulary_profile.py` module: the record file name (`wave.md`), the `wave-id` key, the record title, the `## Wave Summary` and `## Changes` headings, the `Change ID` and `Change Status` labels and the `Wave:` back-reference, plus the tier names. A downstream distribution renames them by editing those constants at merge time, the same way it relocates record roots in `record_paths.py`; nothing is read from configuration, and an invalid profile refuses to import with a message naming the field. Every reader and writer uses the profile (discovery, docs-lint, the lifecycle tools, review evi

dence, memory, the dashboard, the review-policy digest and the Claude Stop hook), and new change documents get the profile's labels. The shipped defaults are today's names, so nothing changes unless a distribution edits them. Run **Upgrade Wavefoundry** (or `wf render-surfaces`) to re-render the Stop hook. Wave `1z8mm`.
- **Record labels may share a prefix.** A vocabulary profile may use labels that are prefixes of one another, such as `Wave`, `Wave ID` and `Wave Status`, because every label is written and read as `Label:` at the start of a line; every reader matches a label only at the start of a line, and a census test keeps it so. The profile refuses duplicate labels, including ones that differ only in case, and a label that differs from a fixed label only in case (for example `status`). The shipped labels are unchanged. Wave `1z8ou`.
- **A read-only archive of older records.** A distribution that renames its record vocabulary can keep its closed records, under their old names, in an archive: set `ARCHIVE_ROOT` in `record_paths.py` and, when the names differ, `ARCHIVE_PROFILE` in `vocabulary_profile.py`. `wf_get_change` and the dashboard document view find archived waves and changes by id (marked archived), and new ids never collide with archived ones. Nothing writes to the archive: lifecycle tools refuse an archived id with `archived_record_read_only`, the docs gardener skips it, and docs-lint checks only that archived records can be read. Both constants are unset by default, so nothing changes unless a distribution sets them. Wave `1z8ts`.
- **Memory backfill reads archived waves.** With a read-only archive configured, memory backfill now inventories and drafts from its closed waves, read with the archive's vocabulary, and writes nothing there; `memory_propose` also accepts an archived wave id. If an archived wave has the same id as a live one, the live wave is used and backfill reports `archived_wave_shadowed`. Nothing changes without an archive. Wave `1z8tz`.

- **A warning when no wave record can be found.** When the waves root holds folders with files but none contains the record file the profile names (for example after a rename), docs-lint warns and `wf_list_waves` and `wf_current_wave` add an advisory `record_file_not_found` diagnostic, instead of reporting no waves without explanation. Folders without files (empty, only subfolders, or only dot-files such as `.gitkeep`) are ignored, so a fresh install or empty grouping folders do not trigger it. Wave `1z8mm`.

### Changed

- **An upgrade or a pull now leaves the required packages installed, or says to run `wf setup`.** When missing or version-incompatible required packages are the only thing stopping the MCP server from starting (typically after a `git pull` of a teammate's committed upgrade), the server now installs them itself: exactly the reported packages, through uv with its 21-day package-age guard (never pip), into the existing tool environment, with nothing written to the MCP output stream and no repository `uv.toml` or `[tool.uv]` settings applied. Packages the server can run without, such as `psutil`, install in the background after it starts; others install before it starts, and if it still cannot start it exits with the `wf setup` guidance. `wf_server_info` reports the install as `startup_install`. One lock now serializes every change to the shared tool environment (creating or recreating it, and every dependency install by `wf setup`, the upgrade and startup); if the lock cannot be taken, nothing is installed, and a check that finds nothing to install takes no lock. The upgrade installs dependencies as its own step before the index update: a failed install is reported as `dependency_provisioning_failed` naming `wf setup`, and the index update is skipped rather than reported as a failed publication. The same handling covers the legacy storage-migration reader: when a storage migration is required and its dependencies cannot be installed, the index phase

fails before anything migrates, keeps the migration receipt and legacy sources, and names `wf setup` (the resume-after-memory path no longer lets that failure escape its own handling). The cleanup summary adds `setup_status`, `setup_reasons` and `setup_command`, and when setup is not ready `wf_upgrade`'s next step recommends the command before reloading. A server running when a pull lands now says its restart will install newly required packages, and the Claude Code session-start hook says the server attempts the install. Operator notes: startup uses the network when a requirement changed, and there is no opt-out; the startup install reads the operator's user-level `uv.toml`, or the system-level one when there is none (uv would merge both); in locked-down environments the install fails within `setup.dep_install_timeout_seconds` and the server reports `wf setup`. The tool environment is shared by every repository on the machine, so two repositories on framework versions with different pins re-pin a package on each host start; on Windows a package in use by another host, an index build or the dashboard cannot be replaced, and the install says what to stop. The upgrade's separate dependency step takes effect from the upgrade after the one that installs it on the default `wf upgrade` and `wf_upgrade()` paths, and the new `wf_upgrade` next step after an MCP reload or restart. ADR `1zcxi-adr startup-dependency-install`. Waves `1zfd9`, `1zep5`.
- **Process information comes from `psutil`.** The MCP server and the indexer now read pid liveness, zombie state, command lines, working directories and start times through one module backed by `psutil`, a new required dependency (`psutil>=6.1,<8`), instead of spawning `tasklist`, `ps` and PowerShell queries. On Windows this replaces branches that had never run on a real Windows host, and process-status calls no longer spawn processes. The MCP server now treats a process it may not signal (for example another user's) as running, an

d a zombie as not running, like the indexer. When a process's start time can be read, a pid recorded by a build and later reused by another process no longer reads as a running build. Dashboard stop no longer deletes the dashboard's lock file: it clears the metadata in place while holding the dashboard's lock, and leaves it untouched when the lock is held or cannot be taken, so a stop racing a starting dashboard can no longer leave two dashboards running. Operator notes: the upgrade installs `psutil` as its own step, and after a `git pull` of a committed upgrade the MCP server installs it at its next start (in the background); `wf setup` also installs it. Until it is installed, readiness reports `dependencies_missing`, `index_health`, `index_build_status` and `wf_server_info` report `process_info_unavailable` recommending `wf setup`, index builds still run (the OS locks decide), and status may show a running build or dashboard as not running. An offline upgrade reports `dependency_provisioning_failed` and skips the index update until `psutil` can be installed. The upgrade that first installs this step does not have it yet: if that install fails, the upgrade completes but reports an index publication failure recommending `index_build`; follow the cleanup summary's `setup_command` (`wf setup`) instead, since `index_build` cannot install a missing package; air-gapped sites can pre-stage the wheel (for example `pip download "psutil>=6.1,<8"` into a local index). On Windows, application control must allow `psutil`'s extension in the tool environment, as it already must for `apsw` and `sqlite-vec`. A change to `process_info.py` takes effect after an MCP server restart, not `wf_reload_mcp`. Wave `1zc7n`.
- **The prompt-surface manifest no longer records a gardening date.** The docs gardener stamped `last_gardened_at` in `docs/prompts/prompt-surface-manifest.json` with the day's date whenever it stamped any other document, so the file changed on every gardening day although

nothing read the date. The gardener no longer writes it and removes it from an existing manifest, so each repository sees a one-time diff that deletes that line, and afterwards the manifest changes only when its content does. Wave `1z8tv`.

### Fixed

- **`wf_upgrade` no longer reports an error after a successful upgrade.** Its automatic post-upgrade reload re-executes the server module during the call, which swapped the context variable the tool wrapper resets, so a successful upgrade or cleanup returned `Token ... was created by a different ContextVar` and agents had to read `.wavefoundry/logs/upgrade.log` to learn the outcome. The wrapper now resets the variable it set. A server running a build without the fix reports the error once, on the call that performs the reload; that reload installs the fixed wrapper, so no restart is needed. Wave `1zeyo`.
- **A crash after the docs gate is labelled as what it is and has a targeted recovery.** A failure in the `post_docs_gate` hook or the memory bootstrap used to be recorded as `failed_phase: awaiting_memory_validation`, the name of the normal historical-memory pause, and `wf_upgrade` reported it as a pre-flight failure; no targeted recovery accepted it, so only a full rerun worked. It is now `failed_phase: post_docs_gate`, `wf_upgrade` names it and points at `wf_upgrade(phase="resume_after_gate")`, and that recovery (also `wf upgrade --resume-after-gate`, and the protocol-bridge package's recovery command) re-runs the docs gate and establishes the memory checkpoint without re-extracting; if that recovery itself fails after the gate, the lock keeps the `post_docs_gate` label so the same command can be retried. When the recovery ends at the normal historical-memory pause, it records that pause the way a full upgrade does, so `wf_upgrade` reports the pause and its next step instead of an error. Index and cleanup refuse such a lock with the same pointer, and the summary reports the docs gate as passed. The recovery also ac

cepts the label an older runner writes for the same crash (`awaiting_memory_validation` with the docs gate complete and no action-required block). `wf_upgrade` identifies the failure from the lock itself, so a server reloaded mid-upgrade still names it correctly. The new label applies from the upgrade after the one that installs it; the recovery runs new code at once. Wave `1zeyo`.
- **An upgrade driven by an older MCP server no longer crashes in the memory step.** Upgrading from 1.27 with `wf_upgrade` from a running 1.27 server failed after the docs gate with `'RecordRoots' object has no attribute 'archive'`: the upgrade's memory hook refreshed only `memory_backfill` while the old server kept its own `record_paths`. The hook now refreshes, in place and leaf-first, every pure framework module the memory bootstrap uses, so the old server's own later import of `memory_backfill` also runs consistent code; modules that hold locks or transactions are never reloaded, and exception classes keep their identity across the refresh so code that imported them by name still catches them. The review-module reloads before the docs gate refresh the same record-layout modules first. This fix is in the upgrade's extension hook, which the running upgrade loads from the new pack, so it applies to the upgrade that installs it, including from 1.27. Wave `1zeyo`.
- **The end of an upgrade no longer repeats finished steps.** The primary `wf_upgrade` call already updates the index, but its next step (and the upgrade prompt) told agents to call `wf_upgrade(phase="update_index")` again before cleanup, which re-ran the whole index update for nothing. It now goes straight to `wf_upgrade(phase="cleanup")`, calling `update_index` first only when the editing pass changed indexed files or the summary reports an index publication failure. Cleanup also no longer ends its log by telling you to run `--update-index` and `--cleanup`: a successful cleanup says the upgrade is complete and lists only the ed

iting-pass steps still to do, and a failed one ends with its recovery instruction. The lifecycle lock file, which stays on disk by design, now records when it was released, so its PID no longer looks like an abandoned lock, and the extraction log names the pack members it withheld instead of only counting them. The shorter sequence applies once the new MCP server is loaded; the upgrade that installs it still shows the old next step, and the withheld names appear from the following upgrade, whose extraction the new runner performs. Wave `1zf1u`.
- **CoreML acceleration survives ONNX Runtime upgrades.** The compiled-model cache for the embedder and reranker was keyed only by the model file's path, so after an ONNX Runtime upgrade that splits the graph differently, the reranker loaded a stale compile, its safety probe failed with `output_features has no value for logits`, and search reranking quietly fell back to the CPU. The cache folder now carries the ONNX Runtime version and a digest of the model graph and CoreML options, so a runtime or model change compiles fresh (once, on the first search or index after upgrading), and superseded compiles for that model are removed, which on an affected Mac frees several hundred megabytes. Removal never follows symlinks or leaves the model's cache folder. Other GPU providers and the CPU path are unchanged. Wave `1zf1w`.
- **The upgrade guidance says when a reload is not enough.** An in-process reload (`wf_reload_mcp`, or the reload `wf_upgrade` runs automatically) re-executes only the implementation module and re-registers the tools; modules the server already imported for indexing, storage, setup and models keep the version the host started with, so the process can run a mix of old and new code. The upgrade prompt used to say ordinary upgrades need only the reload and pointed at `runner_stale`, which covers just `server.py` and `venv_bootstrap.py`, so a `loaded_code_stale` warning after an upgrade read as noise. The prompt and

the cleanup next step now say that `loaded_code_stale` after an upgrade means restart the host. The warning also no longer counts the implementation module itself once a reload has re-executed it, so an upgrade that changed only that module no longer asks for a restart; this part takes effect after the first restart onto this release. Wave `1zf1y`.
- **Code navigation tools no longer read files the index excludes.** When the server could not load the indexer module (for example while an upgrade was replacing it), the tools that walk the working tree (such as `code_list_files`, `code_keyword`, `code_constants`, `code_pattern`, `code_definition`, `code_references` and `code_impact`) fell back to walking every file under the repository, so they listed virtual environments, build output and ignored files, and `code_constants` could return raw bytes from `index.sqlite`. They now keep using the indexer the server already loaded; if the server never loaded one, the tool returns a `navigation_indexer_unavailable` error that says to restart the MCP server. When the index code on disk has changed since the server started, the answer carries an `index_runtime_stale` warning: `wf_reload_mcp` does not load new index code, so restart the server. Wave `1za2y`.
- **`**/` in a navigation glob matches files at every depth.** `code_list_files`, `code_keyword`, `code_constants` and `code_pattern` matched globs with `fnmatch`, where `**/` needs at least one directory, so `**/*.py` skipped top-level files and `src/**/*.py` skipped files directly in `src/`. `**/` now also matches no directory. Globs without `**/` match as before. Wave `1za2y`.
- **`index_build_status` no longer reports a finished background build as running, and checking status no longer releases a build's lock.** The background build was reported `running` whenever the pid in `background-build.pid` was alive, including a finished but unreaped child or a pid now used by another program; it is now `running` only while that

pid is an index build or a `wf setup` / `wf update-indexes` run for this repository. When the MCP server itself held the index build lock (the `fts` rebuild or `index_optimize`), a status check in the same process opened the lock file, which releases a POSIX record lock, so another build could start alongside it. The server now records its own holds in memory, answers `lock.held: true` from that record without opening the file, and refuses a second in-process build. A build that finds a stale lock file now reuses it and rewrites its metadata instead of deleting it first; the deletion raced another build that had just locked the old file, so a third could lock a new file and run alongside it. When the setup process is running but not holding the lock, a `state_note` says `lock.held` is authoritative. When the recorded lock owner is an earlier build or cannot be identified, the conflict message now names `index_build_status` `lock.held` as the check. Wave `1za2y`.
- **The `tags` filter on `docs_search` and `code_search` works again.** Since 1.4 (the move to stored tag filtering), no indexed chunk carried tags, so filtering by `wave`, `agent`, `test` or any other tag returned nothing. The indexer now tags each chunk from its path, following the configured waves root and the archive root, and `memory` is listed in the vocabulary. Operator note: the next index refresh after upgrading re-chunks every file once to add the tags; embeddings are reused, so nothing is re-embedded. If you later change `WAVES_ROOT` or `ARCHIVE_ROOT` without moving files, run `index_build(mode='rechunk')` to re-tag. Wave `1z8tz`.
- **Review ledgers under relocated or nested record roots stay out of retrieval.** Retrieval recognized a wave's `events.jsonl` ledger only at `docs/waves/<wave>/events.jsonl`, so with relocated or nested record roots the raw ledger was indexed as ordinary content. It now uses the configured waves root and depth. Wave `1z8mm`.
- **Fresh installs can start the MCP server

again.** `mcp` 2.x (published 2026-07-28, now past setup's 21-day package-age guard) removed `mcp.server.fastmcp`, so a new `wf setup` installed an `mcp` the server could not import. `mcp[cli]` is now pinned below 2 in the setup requirements and `pyproject.toml`; an environment that already installed 2.x is reported as needing setup, and `wf setup` reinstalls a 1.x release. Wave `1z822`.
- **Seed and framework edit gates work with absolute paths.** The rendered edit hooks compared the host's path with repo-relative prefixes, and Claude Code always sends absolute paths, so on Claude Code the seed and framework-maintenance gates never blocked and the post-edit docs-lint never ran; `..`, `./`, symlinks and case variants slipped past on every host. Every hook now resolves the path against the repository first (case-insensitively where the filesystem is), and a path outside the repository is ignored. Operator note: the gates now block edits they silently allowed before; open them with `wf_open_gate` as the message says. Run **Upgrade Wavefoundry** (or `wf render-surfaces`) to re-render the hooks. Wave `1z822`.
- **Pre-edit hooks fail closed.** A Claude PreToolUse, Copilot pre-tool-use or Windsurf seed-protect hook that could not start (missing `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, or a hook body that raised) exited 1, which hosts treat as a warning, so the edit went through. Post-edit hooks also mark the reindex before reporting a docs-lint failure or a Cursor warning, so an edit that fails lint is still indexed. Wave `1z822`.
- **Lock files never follow a symlink.** A symlink committed at a Wavefoundry lock path could make a lock or metadata write truncate the file it pointed to. Lock carriers are now opened without following a final-component symlink (on Windows, a symlink or reparse point is refused), and a dangling link is refused instead of creating its target. Wave `1z822`.
- **Timed-out helpers end

their whole process tree.** A sensor or MCP helper that timed out had only its direct child killed; a grandchild kept running and, on Windows, could hang the call on pipes it held. Timed sensors and helper subprocesses now start in their own process group and the whole group is ended on timeout. Wave `1z822`.
- **Setup installs, upgrade hooks and the techdocs audit also end their whole process tree on timeout.** The venv, `pip` and `uv` steps of `wf setup`, upgrade convention hook scripts, the upgrade's summary child and graph-builder probe, and the techdocs audit worker killed only their direct child on timeout, so a build, resolver or hook subprocess could keep running, and on Windows the step could hang instead of timing out. They now end the whole process group, and the wait checks for Ctrl-C every half second so an interrupted `wf setup` stops promptly (the Windows behavior follows from the same design but has not been exercised on a Windows host). An upgrade from 1.27.0 keeps working: setup falls back to the previous behavior while the older upgrade runner is the one running it, and the upgrade's own steps are protected from the next upgrade on. Wave `1z8tr`.
- **Timed git commands and system probes end their whole process tree too.** The remaining timed calls to git (the dashboard's git statistics, diffs and changed-file list, the docs gardener's changed-file list, the graph indexer's ignored-path listing, the index freshness, history and drift checks, commit provenance, the techdocs baseline, operator identity, the platform-surface renderer's tracked-runtime check, the retrieval evaluator's provenance probes, the server's working-tree checks and the test runner's repository-state listing) and to system probes and process queries (`sysctl`, `ldconfig`, `nvidia-smi`, `lsof`, `ps`, PowerShell, the CoreML probe and the upgrade import probe) killed only their direct child on timeout, so a git hook or credential helper could keep running. They now end the whole p

rocess group, and fall back to the previous behavior when an older upgrade runner has loaded them. The group is signalled only while the timed-out child has not been reaped, so its id cannot have been reused by an unrelated process. The graph-quality evaluator's provenance probe (`git rev-parse HEAD` and `git status --porcelain`) is routed too, and its shipped reports were re-measured. Waves `1z8ox` and `1za2y`.
- **The framework test suite no longer writes into the repository it runs in.** A census of a full run in a clean clone found a test that updated the secret scanner's skip ledger under `.wavefoundry/index/scan/`, tests that opened the project index in place and left its SQLite `-wal` and `-shm` files behind, and Python children that wrote bytecode next to the scripts. Those tests now write under temporary roots (the index tests read a copy), and the runner sets `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` for every worker. `run_tests.py` also fails a run that creates, modifies or deletes a tracked or non-ignored file, or changes the edit-gate file `.wavefoundry/guard-overrides.json`, names the paths, and writes no receipt; a concurrent edit by an operator or agent during the run trips it too. pl`, the tool registry and the ten handler modules moved from `.wavefoundry/framework/scripts/` into `scripts/wf_server/`. ### Fixed

now shows the hint only when `python3` itself cannot start, and passes every command's exit code through unchanged. Run **Upgrade Wavefoundry** (or `wf render-surfaces`) to re-render the launcher.
- **Required phase sensors can run `npm`, `npx` and `pnpm` on Windows.** A list-form sensor command naming a `.cmd` wrapper failed to start, which blocked wave close. The first element is now resolved through `PATH` and `PATHEXT` on Windows. - **Blocking file locks wait on Windows as they do elsewhere.** They gave up after about ten seconds, so an index build could fail while another writer held the source guard, and the review-evidence publication lock could report itself unavailable. They now wait until the lock is free.

Health reports `spooled_events` and `oldest_spooled_at` without changing its status. Closing a wave replays first; an event it still cannot write marks that wave `accounting_gap` instead of publishing an undercount.

The store-wide gap is now written only when the spool itself cannot take the event. Wave `1z2ma`.
- **One lock timeout no longer blanks Context Efficiency for good.** A context-efficiency write that met a database lock held by another attached MCP server for more than 50 ms wrote the durable accounting gap at once. From then on every wave's `## Context Efficiency` showed `accounting_gap`, with no recorded cause and no supported way out. Busy and locked writes are now retried for up to 10 seconds before the write is given up (and, with the spool above, kept for later). The gap file records when and why it began, and `read_store_health` and its diagnostic report that. `wf clear-accounting-gap` clears it and keeps every wave that lived through the gap marked `accounting_gap`, so no undercount is published as complete. - **The automatic reload after `wf_upgrade` now reaches the running server.** It used to import `server.py` a second time as a new module with no handler, so it reported `handler_not_ready` and the upgraded code was not served until `wf_reload_mcp` or a restart. It now reloads the runner that is serving, and when none is loaded it says the reload was skipped and names `wf_reload_mcp`. The upgrade that installs this fix still runs the previous code, so call `wf_reload_mcp` once afterwards (or restart the MCP host).
- **Upgrade cleanup records the setup baseline even while the index is still updating.** Cleanup used to check setup readiness once; when the post-upgrade reindex was still writing, the check came back `indeterminate` and cleanup skipped the baseline with a misleading warning (the server recorded it at the next start). Cleanup now retries a transient result up to three more times over about 17 seconds, and still never fails the upgrade over it.
- **Setup no longer reports its own inputs as changed.** After an ordinary `wf setup`, `wf setup --check` and the MCP startup notice reported `setup_inputs_changed` on every run, because set

up recorded a provider variable it sets in its own process. The fingerprint now compares only setup-relevant environment fields: the tool environment, the Python version and the operator's provider and reranker settings. Wave `1yzcz`.

  one 1.15 MB identifier-dense evidence artifact cost 173.6 seconds of a 198.5 second full scan. The
  engine now collapses that exact shape to a single span of the combined width at load, in the

nd to a floor shift. Receipts record `warm_floor_ms`, `warm_median_ms`,

ve path gates on

## [1.10.0] - 2026-07-01

### Added

- **`wave_index_optimize` — reclaim on-disk index bloat without re-embedding.** The semantic index tables accumulate on-disk bloat from incremental, edit-driven refreshes (superseded data fragments, stale full-text-search artifacts, old index versions). This new tool runs a tiered ladder — compact in place; if in-place compaction fails because of a LanceDB list-column corruption, rewrite the table fresh (which recomputes offsets and sidesteps the bug) and rebuild its vector and full-text indexes; fall back

to a full rebuild only if a table is entirely unreadable — reclaiming the space with no embedding cost in the common case. It also runs automatically at the end of install and upgrade. A new MCP tool requires a one-time reconnect after upgrade to appear.
- **Index size is visible in `wave_index_health`.** The health response now includes a `size` object — the total on-disk index size plus a per-component breakdown (the docs and code tables and the graph) — so index growth and bloat are diagnosable without shelling out to `du`.
- **`wave_index_build_status` reports an authoritative build-lock state.** The response now carries a `lock` object whose `held` is determined by testing the real operating-system lock (not the presence of the lock file, which persists by design as a last-owner record), plus the last build's owner and whether it finished cleanly or was interrupted. Read `lock.held` to tell whether a build is actually running — do not read the lock file.

### Changed

- **Index refreshes are coalesced to the end of a turn instead of firing on every edit.** Previously each file edit spawned a background reindex; a session of many edits churned the index — and re-grew its on-disk size — continuously. The post-edit hook now marks the index dirty and a single coalesced refresh runs when the turn ends (on hosts with a turn-end hook; other hosts use a longer debounce). The in-session staleness monitor is now a quiet-period safety net — it refreshes only once editing has settled and a recent build has not just run — so the two triggers no longer compete. A new `indexing.monitor.quiet_period_seconds` setting (default 5 minutes) tunes the safety net. Trade-off: semantic search reflects edits made earlier in the same turn only after the turn ends.
- **Embedding precision is provider-aware: half-precision on a GPU, 8-bit on CPU.** The indexer selects embedding precision from the active hardware — FP16 on a GPU/accelerator, INT8 on CPU — for faster indexing with no qualit

y regression, and the reranker follows the same single machine classification so the two never disagree. Small incremental edit batches are routed to the CPU path to skip GPU padding waste, while full rebuilds always use the accelerator.
- **Switching machines no longer forces a needless full re-embed.** The index records the embedding precision *class* (full-precision vs. quantized), so moving a repository between a GPU and a CPU machine re-embeds only when the class actually changes, not on every provider switch.
- **Dependency sync installs pinned version bumps, not just missing packages.** Setup and upgrade now compare installed versions against the pinned specifications and install a newer pin even when the package is already present — so a bumped dependency (such as the LanceDB upgrade in this release) actually lands on upgrade instead of being skipped as "already installed."
- **Index builds self-heal corruption-driven bloat.** When in-place compaction fails because of the LanceDB list-column corruption, the build and the incremental refresh now automatically reclaim the table by rewriting it fresh — so a corrupted table recovers on the next build instead of growing unbounded.
- **Shipped agent guidance no longer references the removed framework index.** Seed prompts and rendered command docs that still described the retired separate "framework" index layer (removed when the framework's own seeds and docs were folded into each project's single index) now state the current single-index reality, so an upgrading repository's agent no longer follows stale guidance.
- **Seed prompts state the journal/persona/manifest structure contracts verbatim.** The seeds that guide an install agent to author agent journals, personas, and the prompt-surface manifest now list the exact required section headings (with case), the per-section bullet rule, the accepted salience markers, the persona `Role:`/`Category:` frontmatter, and the required manifest keys — so an agent produce

s a compliant artifact on the first pass instead of discovering the structure through repeated validation failures.
- **Factor-review reconciliation is self-seeding and no longer noisy on a fresh install.** A fresh install now seeds the factor-review lane set from the repository profile's applicable factors as a prunable default; and when the lane set is left empty while the profile still marks several factors applicable, the audit emits one consolidated, actionable advisory (naming the factors and the remediation) instead of a separate warning per factor on every audit. The review gate still keys off the configured lane set, not the profile.
- **The post-edit docs-lint is incremental.** Docs-lint was the last post-edit reaction that still scanned the whole `docs/` tree on every edit (the index refresh and secret scan were already incremental). The post-edit hook now self-detects the git working-tree changed set and runs only the per-file checks on changed docs; a changed config file falls back to the full lint. The authoritative full corpus lint is unchanged and still runs at prepare, close, install, and upgrade — so a large repo gets fast per-edit feedback without weakening the gate.
- **docs-lint has a configurable file-size guard.** A markdown document larger than `docs_lint.max_file_bytes` (default 5 MB, matching the secret-scan and index file caps) now has its content validators skipped with a single loud, non-blocking warning naming the file, its size, and the remedy — so a pathological multi-megabyte generated document can't stall the regex passes or balloon lint memory, while a legitimately large document never fails the gate.
- **docs-lint reads each file once per run and can report per-phase timings.** The full lint previously re-read the same doc several times (once per validator that touches it); a transparent content cache keyed on file identity removes the redundant reads. A new `--timings` flag reports per-phase wall-clock (secrets/corpus/metadata/li

nks) to help diagnose full-scan cost on large repositories.

### Fixed

- **Index tables no longer accumulate unbounded on-disk bloat.** A full rebuild's finalize now compacts and reclaims the stale index artifacts a rebuild leaves behind (old vector/full-text index versions and data fragments), and incremental refreshes clean reliably — so the on-disk index no longer grows far past its working set over repeated builds.
- **The index-build lock correctly detects a crashed or recycled owner.** The lock's liveness check no longer trusts a bare process-exists signal (which a zombie or a recycled PID could pass), and background index builds launched by the long-running MCP server are now reaped instead of lingering as zombies — so a stale lock is reliably reclaimed on the next build and status surfaces stop reporting a dead build as running.
- **The index-build lock recovery guidance no longer tells you to delete the lock file.** The lock file persists by design as a last-owner record; the early-exit message now points at `wave_index_build_status` to check whether a build is actually running, and the "wait for the running build" case stays actionable.
- **Embedding-model downloads succeed behind a corporate TLS proxy outside of `wf setup`.** The corporate-CA trust bundle was previously applied only during setup's model prewarm; a model download triggered later — by `wave_index_build`, a background index refresh, or the first `code_search` / `code_ask` — ran without it and failed certificate verification behind a proxy. The trust bundle (with a reactive fallback ladder) is now applied at every model-download entry point, so first-use downloads succeed behind a proxy too.
- **LanceDB auto-install no longer fails behind a corporate TLS proxy.** When the indexer auto-installs LanceDB via pip on first use, it now applies the same TLS-conflict mitigation setup already used (removing the exclusive certificate-file variable and enabling native trust), so the auto-install succee

ds behind a proxy instead of failing certificate verification.
- **The post-edit docs-lint gate no longer hangs or fails early on a large repository.** The docs-lint hook ran the linter unbounded (and was capped too low in an earlier build), so on a large docs tree it could stall the editing agent or reject an edit. It now runs under a generous, configurable timeout (`docs_lint.hook_timeout_seconds` in `docs/workflow-config.json`, default 120 s) and treats a timeout as advisory — the edit proceeds and `wave_validate` / wave-close remain the authoritative docs gate — so a slow lint never blocks or hangs the session.
- **The install audit no longer reports a mis-encoded install log as "complete."** When the install log was written by a non-UTF-8 tool (for example Windows PowerShell without `-Encoding utf8`), its em-dash row separators became mojibake and the parser matched zero rows — which then read as vacuously complete. The row parser now tolerates any separator encoding, the completeness check treats an empty parse as not-complete, and the audit reports a distinct "install log unparseable" error instead of silent success; new logs are written UTF-8.
- **docs-lint no longer stalls on large or link-dense documents (and behaves correctly on Windows).** The link checker called a full path-resolution (realpath) for every link in a document — O(links) filesystem syscalls — which on a link-heavy document (a generated reference, a long changelog) on a slower filesystem (Windows/WSL2/network) could take tens of seconds and trip the post-edit hook timeout. It now uses a single lightweight existence check per link (measured ~67× faster on a large synthetic document) with identical results. Separately, relative paths in lint comparisons and messages are now normalized to forward slashes on all platforms, so the historical-doc link-check skips (which used forward-slash prefixes) actually take effect on Windows and lint messages no longer show backslash paths.
- **A journal can

document its own content rules without failing docs-lint.** The check that rejects pasted raw transcripts and secrets no longer fires on a line that is *forbidding* such content — a journal's Governance section naming what it disallows ("Do not include raw transcript content") now passes, while an actual pasted transcript or secret value is still caught. The validator's missing-salience-marker message also now lists the accepted marker vocabulary so the fix is obvious from the error.

> **Two behavior changes to know:** CPU index builds now use a smaller default embedding batch (much lower peak memory — see below), and the local dashboard is now a read-only viewer that no longer runs index builds (the `auto_index` setting was removed; index updates come from the post-edit hook, the MCP server, and `wave_index_build`).

### Added

- **Config-key → reader edges.** A code site that reads a config key by literal name now links to that ke

y in the graph — Python `.get("KEY")`/`cfg["KEY"]` against JSON config, and Java/Spring `@Value("${key}")`/`getProperty("key")` against `application.{yml,properties}` keys (`.properties`/`.yml`/`.yaml` now contribute config-key nodes). Bounded to real config surfaces and unique, distinctive keys so ordinary dictionary access does not create false links.
- **Instrumentation targets on advice classes.** OpenTelemetry `TypeInstrumentation` classes carry an `instruments` property naming the types their `typeMatcher()` weaves into — including `namedOneOf` lists and matchers nested in `implementsInterface`/`hasSuperType` — so "what does this advice instrument" is answerable from the graph without hand-searching. - **Model downloads fall back to the OS trust store.** When a model download fails TLS verification (`CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED`) — common behind a corporate proxy whose root CA is in the OS trust store but not the bundled `certifi` — the fetch retries against the OS trust store (honoring a preset `SSL_CERT_FILE`/`REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`). Verification stays on throughout; only the trusted CA bundle changes.

### Changed

- **Cross-language call-confidence promotion.** A call that resolves to a unique definition by construction (same-file, or an exact cross-file match) is now recorded at full confidence instead of the heuristic tier, across all languages — sharpening blast-radius and change-risk ranking. Only the confidence label changes; no edge target is altered.
- **Transitive blast-radius confidence.** `code_risk_score` propagates edge confidence along the whole path and reports `transitive_extracted_fraction`, so a blast radius reached only through low-trust edges is discounted rather than over-counted.
- **Much lower memory for CPU index builds.** The embedding forward batch is now per-model and defaults to 32 (down from 256), cutting peak RSS of the CPU embedding pass ~3.5–3.8× at equal-or-better throughput (measured on an

M2 Max CPU path). Tune per model via `indexing.code_embed_batch_size` / `docs_embed_batch_size`. The GPU/CoreML path is unaffected. On a constrained low-RAM CPU/WSL2 host this is projected to bring the build well under the memory cap and clear the out-of-memory failure — field-confirmation on such a host is still pending.

### Removed

- **Dashboard `auto_index` / `auto_index_delay_seconds` settings.** The dashboard no longer runs index builds, so these settings were removed; index updates are background/MCP-owned.

The produced index is identical to the previous batch path. Reindex model loads are cached-first (no Hub round-trip on a warm cache), and an incremental update loads only the embedder for a layer that actually changed.
- **Oversized-fil

e guard in the indexer.** Files larger than a hard cap (default 5 MB) are dropped from the index walk, and files over a tree-sitter parse cap (default 2 MB) skip AST graph extraction — bounding index time on pathological inputs such as a large data dump. Every `docs-lint` run and `wave_scan_secrets` MCP call checks tracked files against the ruleset. Findings are recorded in `docs/scan-findings.json` with a `pending → false-positive / suspected-secret / confirmed-secret` lifecycle: `pending` requires classification, `false-positive` requires multi-user confirmation, and `confirmed-secret` requires operator acknowledgment (wave-scoped, re-acknowledgment required per wave). `wave_close` hard-blocks on any `pending` entry and soft-blocks on any unresolved `suspected-secret` or unacknowledged `confirmed-secret`.

. Runs in an isolated subprocess so ProcessPoolExecutor workers and the resource tracker do not bleed into the MCP server process. Auto-escalates to a full scan when the rules hash changes (SHA-256 of both rule files, null-byte separator). Response includes `effective_mode`, `rules_hash_changed`, `escalated_to_full`, `clean`, `elapsed_s`, `total_findings`, `by_status`, `failures_total`, and `failures`.

nt path), and the required-confirmation threshold is clamped down to the number of currently-confirmable (recent, non-bot) reviewers so a lone active maintainer is never deadlocked. The clamp never raises the threshold above the configured policy value.

Shipped in the pack and provisioned into every project on install, and refreshed on upgrade.
- **`code_risk_score` MCP tool.** Ranks the symbols in a scope (path, directory, or glob) by how risky they are to change — a composite of upstream blast radius times log-dampened incoming call-degree (`weighted_affected_file_count * log1p(weighted_fan_in)`). Both terms are weighted by call-edge attribution confidence: heuristic name-based edges count fractionally while type-resolved edges count in full, so a ubiquitous accessor name (`getKey`, `getValue`, `toString`) can't top the ranking purely on a name collision with an unrelated symbol. Each result also carries the raw `affected_file_count`/`fan_in` and an `extracted_edge_frac

tion` so a high-but-mostly-heuristic score is visibly discountable. `fan_out` (what the symbol itself calls) is surfaced as an independent component, not folded into the score. The response carries `score_formula` and `score_components` so the ranking is transparent and re-weightable; `top` caps the result and a candidate-cap guard asks to narrow the scope rather than running an unbounded per-symbol traversal. It ranks *many* symbols across a scope, where `code_impact` sizes *one*.

- **Constant retrieval across all languages.** Module-, class-, and type-level constants are now chunked for semantic search and emitted as graph nodes in every supported language, with a function→constant `reads` edge (faithfulness-gated: same-scope or explicitly-imported only, never a coincidental same-name twin). `code_definition` resolves a constant by name, `code_references` lists its readers in a distinct `reads` bucket (not merged into callers), and `code_ask` surfaces constants alongside code. `reads` is opt-in for default graph traversal so a hot constant does not balloon neighbor sets.

### Changed

- **Scan auto-escalation in indexer.** `update_secrets_scan()` escalates to a full scan on scanner-version mismatch, missing findings file, or rules-hash change — previously only version mismatch and missing file triggered escalation.
- **Scanner skips files it should never scan.** Binary files (null-byte sniff), files larger than 5 MB, and individual lines longer than 32 KB are skipped and recorded as skips rather than scanned — bounding scan time and avoiding garbage matches on minified or generated blobs. Default `[allowlist].paths` now also cov

er common generated artifacts (lockfiles, minified bundles, vendored trees) and binary extensions.
- **Fewer false positives in prose and on structural noise.** The `generic-api-key` rule is scoped in Markdown/docs prose by a path clause plus an entropy ceiling and a prose-shape signal, so ordinary documentation sentences no longer trip it. The global `[allowlist]` `regexes`/`stopwords` value-filters now apply across every rule, suppressing `$VAR`, `{{template}}`, `%FMT%`, `/Users/…`-path and similar structural-noise values. Overlapping matches on the same secret are de-duplicated, and matches on comment lines are flagged for triage rather than auto-suppressed.
- **Tighter redaction of short secrets.** `matched_text` redaction is length-scaled — short values expose at most a 2+2 window and never more than ~40% of characters; the wider 4+4 window applies only at length ≥ 20. Raw secrets are never written to the ledger.
- **Clearer secrets-gate failure handling.** A docs-gate failure on a secrets finding now states which findings block, their status, and how to resolve them, and the upgrade flow routes the operator to the resolution loop before retrying the gate.
- **Project secrets policy is materialized before the first upgrade gate.** The upgrade flow writes `docs/scan-rules.toml` (committer-derived confirmation threshold) before the first docs gate runs, so the common "policy file missing" case can no longer fail the gate. The later editing-pass step is now an audit that only completes the rarer "file exists but lacks the policy key" case.
- **Full-scan reconciliation of stale findings.** A full secrets scan now drops `pending` findings the current ruleset no longer produces — e.g. after a rule or allowlist change has since suppressed them — so a ruleset improvement no longer leaves a phantom `pending` entry blocking `wave_close`. Strictly `pending`-only: operator classifications (`false-positive` / `suspected-secret` / `confirmed-secret`) are never auto-removed,

and incremental scans (which re-evaluate only changed files) never prune.
- **Cross-file calls through Python sibling-script loaders now resolve.** Calls reached through the lazy `_load_script("module")` loader idiom — a module obtained via a thin loader wrapper, then called as `loaded.Class.method()` or `loaded.func()` — now resolve to the loaded module's symbols instead of emitting no edge at all. This closes a blast-radius blind spot where heavily-called symbols (reached only through the loader) reported zero incoming calls, so `code_impact` and `code_risk_score` now see their true reach.
- **Ambiguous cross-file receivers are disambiguated by import.** When a method call's receiver type shares its simple name with classes in other packages, the call is now resolved to the class the source file actually imported (using the file's import edges), instead of staying unresolved on the name collision. Applies where a per-type import carries the receiver name — Python `from a import Foo` and Java/Kotlin single-type imports. Unique-name cross-file calls already resolved; this fixes the same-name-collision case.
- **Cross-file method resolution extended to Go, Rust, C#, and same-package Java/Kotlin.** Go methods are keyed by receiver type (`Type.method`), and a package-qualified receiver (`var h foo.Helper`) resolves to the method in the named package — matched by the candidate's package directory, and left external when no project package matches. Rust associated functions (`Bar::build()`) and struct-literal / `::new()` let-bindings resolve to their type. C# calls across namespaces disambiguate by namespace membership — the caller's own declared namespace (read from the file's namespace declarations, so a caller in a nested class resolves correctly) plus its `using` directives. A same-package / same-directory fallback resolves Java/Kotlin/Go receivers used without an import. Every path binds only a unique package- or namespace-faithful candidate and otherwise leaves the

call external — it never binds a wrong same-named twin.
- **Cleaner import edges for Rust, Kotlin, Go, Swift, and C.** Import extraction no longer emits junk `external::<keyword>` edges. The grammar root node was being mis-detected as an import (it shares a substring with an import keyword), which regexed entire files into one edge per token; statement keywords such as `import`, `use`, and `as` also leaked. Rust `use` declarations now produce clean dotted module targets with `as` aliases honored.
- **`code_impact` graph mode bounds its edge list.** The `edges` array is capped at `max_results` (with `edges_total` reporting the true count) so a high-fan-in symbol no longer blows the response past the tool's token limit, and the graph-mode `resolved` field is populated instead of returning null.

- **Upgrade lock no longer strands a half-replaced tree.** A docs-gate failure mid-upgrade records the failed phase and leaves a recoverable lock instead of a stuck in-progress marker, so the dashboard and the next upgrade invocation detect and resume the interrupted upgrade rather than reporting a healthy state over a partially-migrated tree.
- **Correct upgrade version resolution and prune reporting.** `from_version` is resolved from the installed framework revision (manifest `framework_revision`, with `VERSION` fallback) consolidated in one place, and the upgrade's prune count is read from the prune step's actual output rather than mis-derived — so the summary reports the real number of removed files.
- **Lifecycle IDs dedup across plans, waves, and ADRs.** ID minting now scans existing plan, wave, and ADR prefixes together when choosing the next available prefix, so a new plan, wave, or ADR can no longer collide with an ID already issued in a sibling family.
- **26 silently-dead secret detectors revived.** The ruleset is Gitleaks-schema (RE2), and 26 of its regexes used syntax Python's `re` rejects — an inline `(?i)` flag placed mid-pattern, and the `\z` end-of-text ancho

r — so they failed to compile and were silently skipped, leaving their secret types undetected (Adobe, SendGrid, Slack session cookies, Sentry, PlanetScale, Postman, Linear, GoCardless, Facebook page tokens, Alibaba, Authress, and more). A load-time RE2→Python translation shim now adapts these patterns faithfully (inline flags relocated to scoped groups preserving their original scope, `\z`→`\Z`) — applied only to patterns that fail to compile, so the already-valid rules are untouched and the ruleset stays Gitleaks-schema for future imports.

### Removed

- **Canonical-names rename manifest retired.** The `canonical-names.json` rename manifest and its docs-lint alias machinery are removed. `docs/workflow-config.json` must use the canonical keys (`wave_implement`, `wave_review`); docs-lint no longer accepts the legacy spellings, no longer escalates them by version, and no longer warns on retired role slugs. A one-shot convergence migration still rewrites the legacy config keys (`wave_execution` → `wave_implement`, `wave_council_policy` → `wave_review`) to canonical on every upgrade, so existing projects converge automatically; that migration is itself slated for removal at 2.0.0. The runtime `wave_council_policy` reader-fallback is removed. This pulls the previously-published 2.0.0 config-key removal forward. See ADR `1p5be`.

# Data and Control Flow

Owner: Engineering
Status: active
Last verified: 2026-10-30

## Runtime advisory boundary

`runtime_advisory.py` derives nonblocking advice from the executing interpreter and returns data without printing or changing environment state. `wf_cli.main` owns one stderr notice per command invocation; the executable MCP serving entry in `server.py` owns one per server process. MCP help and dry-run verification stay silent for this notice, preventing a duplicate during setup. Imports, hot reloads, tool handlers and readiness monitors do not emit it.

`setup_readiness.assess_setup` includes the data in `advisories`, separate from reasons and actions. Existing status, startup blocking, text formatting and exit-code decisions remain unchanged. Index health exposes the assessment for agents whose host hides stderr.

## Primary Control Paths

### Optional inference service

`inference_provider.py` reads the distribution-owned `inference_profile.py` for
every selection. The default delegates to the existing Tensorwell client; local-only
selection returns the existing local fallback; an explicit extension loads its
declared flat helper and validates both capabilities before use. Setup and indexing
use the same facade outside MCP. Extension factories and operations receive finite
monotonic deadlines; their trusted transports enforce them, and late or malformed
results are refused with fixed nonsecret errors. No failed extension request retries
another provider. Existing search/lexical degradation still reports unavailable
inference and does not construct a replacement model.

The server reload evicts the facade and declaration with other framework routing
modules, and the existing helper inventory reloads the adapter and reports its source
digest. The profile and facade are explicit members of the core script and setup
source inventories. Implementation reload executes their exact source bytes and
refreshes their launch digests only when pre/post source ha

shes agree. Before reload,
a changed profile or facade is reported as stale; after reload its current routing is
represented by the updated identity. Model compatibility pins remain bound to the
loaded index runtime and require restart when changed.
Selection and actual execution reuse the existing status fields with a bounded public
provider label. Status itself performs no adapter or network work.

Actual MCP serving enters the FastMCP lifespan and schedules a once-per-process
Tensorwell discovery/start worker; tool registration does not wait for it. The worker
uses a qualified installed controller only for a bounded start of the existing
configuration. Client deadlines terminate/reap only the exact owned CLI child and grant
no authority over the shared daemon. Ready services can also be reused by standalone
index/setup processes, whose imports never initiate startup. Inference selection and
raw query/document roles are specified in [Embedding model](embedding-model.md#optional-tensorwell-execution-wave-20nju).
Compact server-info status reads cached client state without a fresh probe.

Implementation reload refreshes the client in place while preserving its process-owned
locks, startup-once flag and any existing startup worker. It invalidates the qualified
pair cache; discovery or inference from the previous client generation cannot publish
new cached state or return service output. The existing worker keeps its original
deadline, and reload never schedules another start or stops the shared service.

### MCP process lifetime and cleanup

The agent host owns each stdio connection and its server process lifetime.
`wf_reload_mcp` updates the implementation and handler inside that same process;
it does not replace Python or disconnect another session. `wf_server_info` and
reload expose `data.process` with PID, parent PID, project root and monotonic
uptime since the first server implementation import. Uptime survives reload.
The explicit reload result says whether the

implementation changed and that the
process was not restarted. Runner changes still require a host restart.

Reload first pauses monitor callback admission under a shared condition and waits
up to one second for active callbacks to drain. Admission and active bookkeeping
use the same condition; callback bodies execute outside it, and their active
interval includes status/error processing. If preparation times out or raises,
the pause is released without stopping workers or disposing handler resources.
The blocked callback continues; ordinary scheduling resumes without a reload.
Preparation refusal reports phase `prepare` and `handler_preserved: true`.
Successful preparation keeps admission paused until cleanup stops the workers.
This budget covers preparation waiting, not the existing public reload tool's
telemetry projection work. It does not quiesce arbitrary foreground tool calls.

The serving lifespan finalizer resolves and closes the current handler, including
a handler installed by reload, on normal exit or serving exception/cancellation.
`ImplHandler.close` attempts the two monitor stops, telemetry close and cache
invalidation independently, clears index references and reports named failures.
Each monitor join waits at most one second; a surviving worker retains its
thread and stop-event references for retry. Reload refuses before module
re-execution or handler replacement when cleanup is incomplete, leaving the same
handler installed. Other independent resources may already have been released;
this is a retryable cleanup failure (phase `cleanup`, `handler_preserved: false`),
not a promise of uninterrupted service. Failures after destructive cleanup begins
are not rolled back; the preservation guarantee applies only to preparation.
Shutdown failures are reported on stderr without replacing the serving error.

EOF regression coverage includes idle serving, repeated reload and finite active
work. It does not promise immediate interruption of arbitrary blocking

/native
work or graceful cleanup after SIGKILL. A quiet host-held connection is not proof
of abandonment: Wavefoundry adds no idle killer or cross-session process sweep.
Cleanup never stops Tensorwell's shared daemon or menu application. If cleanup
continues to fail, restart the MCP connection through its host when other work
on that host can be interrupted.

### Lifecycle response completion

The four native create, prepare, implement and close handlers construct their core
response, then pass through `_lifecycle_context_result`. An explicitly declared
`EXTENSION_LIFECYCLE_RESPONSE_CALLBACKS` helper receives detached response/argument
copies at that point, before context-efficiency recording and checkpoint projection.
Its bounded JSON mapping occupies only `data.extension_response`; callback failures
add a bounded advisory without changing core publication truth or retrying writes.

Mutating calls keep their existing project publication hold until completion returns.
Preview retains its existing nonmutating behavior without that hold. An early return
that never reaches completion has no callback; unsupported tools have no late fallback.
Canonical aliases and overrides that delegate to the core reach this boundary once per
core execution. The helper uses the existing declared-source loader, provenance and
reload cleanup; no extra scan, evidence file, approval step or network work is added.
The callback is trusted synchronous code, not a sandbox, deadline or rollback boundary.

### Read-only lifecycle inspection during a retained upgrade

Only the native Prepare `dry_run`/`evaluate` and close-wave `dry_run` paths may inspect a retained upgrade. The registration guard binds the actual arguments and checks the native handler identity; canonical aliases use the same route, while replacement handlers and other publishers retain the guard. A private call context skips the lifecycle lock, completion callback, focus and accounting publication only after bounded checkpoint c

ompatibility and loaded-code checks pass. Validation still runs once; no upgrade continuation, indexing, model startup or checkpoint changes occur.

The checkpoint check accepts supported protocol and legacy memory shapes, extension phase names, and checks repository identities when supplied. It compares installed VERSION with recorded versions and uses the existing loaded-source and ordered runner digest formats through capped no-follow reads. These local read adapters must stay aligned with `setup_readiness`'s source inventory/schema and the runner's two launch files. This proves advisory shape/current-code compatibility, not pack integrity, resume authority or upgraded readiness. Unreadable, incompatible or stale state refuses with `upgrade_preview_unavailable` and preserves the checkpoint.

The child uses `docs-lint --read-only` with bytecode disabled and no inherited cache prefix. This full assessment performs the existing checks but publishes neither scanner findings nor skip observations. Newly detected secret findings are returned as failures with an explicit unpublished notice, so a close preview cannot mistake an unchanged findings ledger for a clean scan. There is no second scan. `--changed`, advisory incremental options and `--write-migration-audit` are incompatible with `--read-only`. Ordinary no-upgrade previews retain their existing observation/callback behavior.

### Path 1: Lifecycle ID Generation

## Runtime Lock Convention

Dedicated project-runtime OS-lock carriers live under `.wavefoundry/locks/`:
the dashboard launch mutex and lifetime/metadata carrier, the project-state
publication lock, and context-efficiency producer leases under `locks/producers/`.
`runtime_lock.py` is the mechanical authority for lazy parent creation, binary
open, POSIX/Windows acquire and release, byte ranges, typed busy versus I/O
outcomes, held probing, handle closure, and in-place JSON metadata. Lock files
persist after release; pathname existence never proves a live holder.

Record-style locks (the lifecycle and index-build locks) are open file
description (OFD) locks on Linux and macOS with a 64-bit interpreter on x86_64
or arm64 (wave `1zxnz`), so an unrelated open and close of the lock file in the
holding process cannot release them. Elsewhere, or when the kernel or filesystem
rejects OFD as unsupported, they fall back to classic `lockf`, decided per
acquire; a busy OFD result is busy and never falls back. OFD and `lockf` locks
exclude each other, so older processes stay excluded during an upgrade. Each
lock records its `mechanism` (`ofd`, `lockf`, `flock` or `msvcrt`) and releases
with it. `runtime_lock.py` also owns the per-platform `struct flock` layout, and
holds the in-process hold registry; `wf_reload_mcp` reloads it in place, state
preserved, keeping the registry, its guard and its exception classes, before any
evicted module is re-imported.

Resource wrappers retain policy. Dashboard code owns check → launch-lock →
recheck → spawn → lifetime-lock ordering; review evidence owns same-thread
re-entrancy; context-efficiency owns producer abandonment and reap; the indexer
owns stale-owner, F_GETLK holder-PID, `ended_at`, and interrupted-

build
interpretation. `.wavefoundry/index/index-build.lock` therefore remains
co-located with the nuke-and-rebuild index resource, while
`.wavefoundry/upgrade-in-progress.json` remains a root-level transaction/state
marker rather than an OS-lock carrier. SQLite locks intrinsic to their
resource files and the framework test-run lock are outside this path convention.

Upgrade performs a one-way cutover with no runtime fallback. Before extraction,
the new pack's upgrade extension records dashboard restart intent, stops the
installed dashboard, proves the old dashboard/publication/producer carriers are
not held, and deletes those old paths. The extracted runtime recognizes only
`.wavefoundry/locks/`. Cleanup restarts a previously running dashboard on its
prior port before removing the upgrade marker; restart failure retains the
marker and intent for recovery. Every creator provisions its own lock parent,
so fresh installs and upgraded projects do not require eager directory setup.

generation), a monotonic `generation`, and a `memory_writers` table of **writer-owned fence tokens**. **Writers:**
the `memory_*` tools (`memory_fence` registers a unique token BEFORE the filesystem write; `memory_finalize`
removes ONLY that token and advances the generation AFTER) and the indexer (`memory_invalidate` runs early — right
after the changed/removed path sets are known, before any vector/FTS/freshness/drift work — when a memory record
changed on disk via a hook/raw edit). **Readers** (the hot-path advisory cache) key on
`(epoch, generation, dir_mtime)` and BYPASS caching whenever the store is unreadable or any *live* writer token
exists (`read_memory_state` synthesizes a `dirty` flag from the live-token count, so the reader key contract is
unchanged). **Writer-owned tokens (not a shared flag):** a single shared `dirty` flag let one writer's finalize
clear a concurrent writer's fence (A fence, B fence, A finalize → cleared while B still mutating). Each writer owns
its token and finalize deletes only its own, so B's fence survives A's finalize. A crashed writer's token is
bounded by a TTL (`_MEMORY_WRITER_TTL_SECONDS`, 300s): readers stop bypassing on tokens older than the TTL
(self-heal) and the rw paths lazily reap them. **Failure semantics:** if the fence cannot be registered the tool
REFUSES the mutation; if a finalize fails, the token rema

warm-cache performance) until the next successful mutation or the TTL. The indexer's `memory_invalidate` returns
True ONLY when the generation DURABLY advances (the sole durable invalidation for a raw content edit, which leaves
`dir_mtime` unchanged); on failure it sets a best-effort short-lived fence token and returns False, and the
**build then FAILS before recording file metadata** (`_build_failed_result`) so the edited record's old file_meta
is preserved and the recovered retry re-detects the edit and advances the generation — a "clean" build can never
strand a warm reader on the pre-edit advisory. The store is derived/rebuildable — deleting it only forces cache
reloads.

`GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE`/`GIT_COMMON_DIR`/…, object-graph *interpretation* `GIT_SHALLOW_FILE`/`GIT_GRAFT_FILE`/
`GIT_REPLACE_REF_BASE`/`GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS`, and config injection `GIT_CONFIG*`) unioned with a hardcoded
fallback superset, so a newer git that adds a local var is covered without a code change. **Protected GLOBAL/SYSTEM
config is passed through unchanged** — it is deliberately NOT neutralized, because git only accepts `safe.directory`
trust from protected scope, and discarding it would break ordinary shared/differently-owned checkouts (containers,
C

I mounts, WSL, shared workspaces) with a "dubious ownership" failure. Instead, the one parser-critical setting —
rename detection — is pinned per-command with `--no-renames` on the freshness and history walks (command flags

config sledgehammer. This closes three failure modes: an inherited `GIT_DIR=/missing` no longer makes a valid repo
report "not a git repository" (authority mis-read); an ambient `GIT_DIR` pointing at an unrelated DECOY repo can no
longer redirect the downstream history/freshness/blob reads to the decoy; and an ambient `GIT_SHALLOW_FILE`/

fallback. A structural AST census test asserts no process-spawn (`subprocess.run`/`Popen`/aliases/variable-built
commands) exists outside `_run_git`. A `confirmed_non_git` result requires BOTH the POSITIVE "`not a git repository`"
fatal (matched under a forced C locale) AND the genuine ABSENCE of any `.git` marker at the root or an ancestor

or an unreadable marker, and those are PRESENT-BUT-INVALID repos — not non-git trees — so a present marker forces

unexpected output — is also `probe_failed`, NOT confirmed non-git**, so none can authorize a destructive clear. A
FRESH non-git project has nothing to clear, but a git-built index copied into — or a repo that dropped its git
metadata under — a now-non-git root would otherwise keep serving stale git-derived `drifted: true` rows. So on a
CONFIRMED non-git transition the git-derived wave attribution +

transactionally CLEARED (`IndexStateStore.clear_attribution_and_drift`, idempotent). A `probe_failed` result
